At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d551:
In the flow of wartime mail, Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons wrote to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 5 June 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the early summer of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d651:
On 30 October 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0000051:
Anthony M. Giannetti, Peter M. Snow, Olga Zak, and co-workers published this study in PLOS Biology in 2003. It asks how the human transferrin receptor can bind more than one partner. That receptor sits on cell surfaces and pulls iron into cells by catching transferrin, the blood protein that carries iron.

A receptor that must catch iron-loaded transferrin, let go at the right time, and still deal with other binders needs a neat trick. The authors work out the shape and contact points that let one receptor handle these jobs. The result helps explain how cells control iron intake. That process matters for blood health. It also matters in diseases where iron builds up or runs short.
plos-pbio-0020351:
Richard W. R. Retallick, Hamish McCallum, and Rick Speare surveyed a frog disease in Australia in PLOS Biology in 2004. A fungus called chytrid has driven sharp frog declines worldwide. The team checked a frog community after its decline, to see whether the fungus was still present.

It was: the fungus persisted at low levels in the surviving frogs, a state called endemic infection. That finding changes the recovery picture. Frogs that remain are not free of the threat; they live with it. Some species may have gained tolerance, while others stay rare. For conservation, the message is that saving such communities means managing a lasting disease, not waiting for it to pass.
plos-pone-0000151:
Claudia Hetzer, Dwayne Bisgrove, Michael S. Cohen, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines how the viral protein Tat recruits and switches on RSK2, an enzyme inside human cells. Tat is the protein HIV uses to drive production of more virus from an infected cell.

By tracing Tat's grip on RSK2, the authors map one step in HIV's takeover of cell machinery. Each such step is a possible place for a drug to intervene. The paper adds detail to the picture of how the virus borrows host enzymes, knowledge that antiviral design depends on.
plos-pone-0000251:
Dario L. Ringach published this theoretical neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks where the functional architecture of the cortex comes from. These are the orderly maps in the brain's outer layer, where neighboring neurons respond to similar features of the world. The author proposes an account of how that organization originates.

Cortical maps are among the most striking patterns in the brain, and their origin has been debated for decades. The paper argues for a developmental explanation rooted in the statistics of input and wiring. It is a theory piece, meant to organize data and provoke tests, rather than report a new experiment.
plos-pone-0000351:
Jules B. Panksepp, Kimberly A. Jochman, Joseph U. Kim, and colleagues published this mouse behavior paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Adolescent mice vary genetically in how social they are. The authors report that affiliative behavior, ultrasonic communication, and social reward are all influenced by genetic variation in these young mice.

Mice talk ultrasonically and find company rewarding, much as social mammals do. Showing genes sway those traits makes the mouse a model for the biology of sociability. The work is relevant to research on conditions marked by social differences, where genetic effects are strong but hard to study in people.
plos-pone-0000451:
Sukanya Narasimhan and colleagues vaccinated against tick saliva itself, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The black-legged tick Ixodes scapularis spreads Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia bacteria. The team targeted salivary proteins the tick injects within 24 hours of attachment, aiming to build immunity against those early proteins.

The title states the strategy worked: immunity thwarted tick feeding and impaired Borrelia transmission. A vaccine that stops the tick from feeding could block several tick-borne diseases at once, not just one germ. The study supports anti-tick vaccines as a different line of defense, aimed at the carrier rather than the disease.
plos-pone-0000551:
Scott R. Evans and colleagues tested a drug for HIV-related nerve pain with the help of an electronic diary, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. HIV-associated sensory neuropathies cause burning pain in the feet and hands. Their randomized trial evaluated Prosaptide for this condition, while patients recorded neuropathic pain in an electronic diary rather than from memory at clinic visits.

Pain is subjective and fades in recall, so real-time diaries measure a drug's effect more honestly. A randomized trial built on such records sets a higher standard for pain claims. Even the measurement method here is part of the contribution to a difficult field.
plos-pone-0000651:
Pengyuan Liu, Haris Vikis, Yan Lu and co-authors mapped complex traits in mice by computer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Understanding the genetics of common diseases and their measurable traits should aid diagnostics and treatments. Mice offer rich genome and trait data gathered in many separate resources. Bringing those resources together quickly could speed gene discovery.

Their approach is in silico mapping at large scale, meaning computation across inbred mouse strains rather than new breeding. Inbred strains differ in known ways, so trait differences can be matched to genome differences. A validated shortcut like this saves years, and its hits point biologists to candidate genes for lab testing.
plos-pone-0000751:
Tara G. Martin, Iadine Chadès, Peter Arcese and colleagues asked how to spend conservation money on animals that will not stay put. Migratory species make up a significant portion of the world's biodiversity, and annual conservation investment in them exceeds several billion dollars. Designing effective plans is enormously challenging, because migrants are influenced by events across whole routes and seasons.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study seeks the optimal conservation of migratory species. Optimal means deciding where protection buys the most survival: breeding grounds, wintering grounds, or the stops between. A species can be guarded carefully in one country and lost in another. This work frames that allocation as a solvable problem.
plos-pone-0000851:
Komla Sobo, Isabelle Le Blanc, Pierre-Philippe Luyet and co-authors showed how cholesterol stuck inside cell compartments jams the cell's internal traffic. In Niemann-Pick type C, a storage disease that harms the brain, cholesterol builds up in late endosomes. Endosomes are small sacs that sort and move material a cell takes in. The team studied sick cells, and healthy cells dosed with a drug that copies the defect.

They tracked how the buildup changes the endosome membrane and slows traffic within it. Their title states the result plainly: the buildup leads to impaired intra-endosomal trafficking. If sorting stalls, the cell starves amid plenty. That jam helps explain the wide cell damage seen in this disease.
plos-pone-0001051:
Peter Mohler, Jane Healy, Hui Xue and colleagues described a heart gene variant set with a balanced trade off, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene ANK2 makes ankyrin-B, a scaffold that organizes heart cell proteins. Certain variants are common: about two percent in Europeans and up to eight percent in West African groups, by the authors' figures.

The team call the pattern ankyrin-B syndrome. The variants enhance cardiac function yet carry a risk of cardiac death and early senescence, cell aging. A variant kept common by an advantage while carrying a late cost is a classic evolutionary balance. The report reframes these carriers from patients to a trade off case.
plos-pone-0001151:
A piece of tissue mixes many cell types, so measuring its gene activity gives an average that can hide what any one type is doing. Konstantin Khodosevich, Dragos Inta, and Peter Seeburg addressed that problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They worked with cells made fluorescent inside living animals, so the cells of interest glow and can be picked out.

The authors describe gene expression analysis of these labeled cells, comparing approaches such as laser microdissection for isolating a cell type. Their method gives cleaner profiles of single cell populations. That precision helps researchers connect genes to the specific cells that use them.
plos-pone-0001251:
Bevirimat is a drug that blocks HIV at an unusual step: maturation, the final assembly step that makes new virus particles infectious. Cheryl Stoddart and colleagues tested it in mice carrying human thymus and liver tissue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The compound, also called PA-457, showed activity at very low concentrations against many wild-type and drug-resistant HIV-1 isolates.

The authors report potent activity of bevirimat against HIV-1 in these SCID-hu Thy/Liv mice, a standard preclinical model. A drug with a novel mechanism is valuable because it can work where existing drugs fail. The mouse results supported moving the compound toward human study.
plos-pone-0001351:
Aging is accompanied by a low-grade rise in inflammatory signals throughout the body. Magnus Bäck and colleagues asked whether the mouth is one site of that chronic inflammation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. A variety of locally released mediators and inflammatory cells had been reported in the human oral cavity.

The authors investigated the presence of inflammatory mediators in the oral cavity across ages. The mouth is an accessible window on systemic inflammation, and it is also where gum disease develops. Their findings bear on whether oral inflammation is part of aging itself or a separate, treatable process.
plos-pone-0001451:
Kuo Ching Chao and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a new source of insulin making cells. People with type 1 diabetes lack such cells, and donor supply is short. The team took stem cells from the jelly of human umbilical cords. These cells are easy to get and to process, unlike embryo cells.

They guided the cord cells to form clusters much like the islets of the pancreas. Such clusters are the body's insulin factories. If they work after transplant, they could help control blood sugar. The work is an early step, but it names a rich and low cost cell source to test further.
plos-pone-0001551:
Teruaki Nakatsuji and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a shot aimed at acne. Acne hits more than fifty million people in the United States alone. Its weight tracks the immune reply to a skin germ that lives in pores. Standard care uses germ drugs or skin peels. The team aimed a vaccine at a surface enzyme of that germ.

Blocking that enzyme could blunt the germ's harm without broad germ drugs. A shot for acne would be a new class of care for a very common ill. The work is a first step, testing the aim in lab models. It opens a path worth a close watch.
plos-pone-0001651:
Maria Teresa Landi and co-authors searched smokers' lung tissue for a gene activity pattern tied to cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Smoking causes more than 90 percent of lung cancers, yet the exact gene changes it drives, and how they shape survival, were still unclear. The team focused on lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of the disease.

They measured gene activity with Affymetrix chips in samples from 135 people and looked for a signature that marks smoking's effect. The full text gives the gene lists, how the pattern tracked with cancer growth, and how it related to patient survival. A clear signature could one day help doctors judge risk or pick treatments for smokers who develop lung tumors.
plos-pone-0001751:
Daniel J. Kelley, Terrence R. Oakes, Larry L. Greischar, and their co-authors built software to clean brain scan noise in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Resting-state functional MRI studies look at slow neural fluctuations. Breathing and heartbeat create fluctuations in the same low frequency range, muddying the signal. Labs lacked automated tools to process the physiological signals recorded at high rates during scans.

Their software processes those waveforms automatically for noise correction and analysis. The full text gives the pipeline, the test scans, and how much cleaner the brain signals became. Routine cleanup of heart and lung noise makes resting-state studies more reliable across labs, which matters as such scans enter clinical research.
plos-pone-0001851:
Julie Lozier, Brent McCright, and Thomas Gridley studied bile duct formation in mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Alagille syndrome is a developmental disorder caused predominantly by mutations in Jagged1, a gene encoding a ligand for Notch family receptors. A characteristic feature is intrahepatic bile duct paucity: too few bile ducts inside the liver.

Building on their earlier work with mutant mice, the team shows Notch signaling regulates bile duct morphogenesis, the shaping of the duct network. The full text gives the mouse genetics and liver images. Children with Alagille syndrome can need liver transplants, so knowing the pathway that builds ducts guides both diagnosis and any future regenerative approach.
plos-pone-0001951:
Gurinder Atwal and co-authors used information theory to sort cancer risk factors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Inherited genes, sex, and hormone signals all shape the risk of cancer and how it grows. How these factors interact in one patient was hard to weigh, yet the mix may decide who gets ill and how fast.

The team applied tools from information theory, which measure how much one fact tells about another, to data from cancer patients. Their aim was to weigh genes, gender, and age side by side. A clear ranking of these forces could sharpen prevention and help aim treatment at the risks that count most.
plos-pone-0002051:
Mark Humphries and Kevin Gurney gave network science a stricter ruler, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many networks, in technology, biology, society, and information, are called small-world. Their nodes form tight clusters, yet the average path between nodes is as short as in a random graph with the same counts.

Loose use of the label made unlike networks sound the same. The pair offer a quantitative method, small-world-ness, that scores how small-world a network truly is against the random match. A number, rather than a slogan, lets fields as far apart as brain science and the web compare networks fairly.
plos-pone-0002151:
Melissa Thomas and Leigh Simmons tested a prediction from sperm competition theory in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. When females mate with many males, each male faces rivals whose sperm compete to fertilize eggs. Theory says males should adjust how much they invest in each mating based on how strong that rivalry is.

One version of the theory says that whether rival males are close kin should change that choice. Thomas and Simmons report that relatedness among rivals did not shift ejaculate allocation as predicted. A clear negative result like this one helps refine what males actually respond to when they adjust their effort.
plos-pone-0002251:
Endre Majorovits, Mohamed Nejmeddine, Yuetsu Tanaka, and co-authors took close-up pictures of a virus passing from cell to cell, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Human T-lymphotropic virus 1 spreads by direct contact between cells, across an organized junction called a virological synapse. Light microscopy had shown the synapse exists, but its fine structure stayed hidden.

Using electron tomography, which builds a 3D view from many electron microscope images, the team visualized the virus at the synapse in detail. Seeing the handed-over particles up close may reveal weak points where drugs or antibodies could block this hidden route of infection.
plos-pone-0002351:
Adam Fisher and Matthew DeLisa evolved a faster-folding version of the green fluorescent protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. GFP glows green and is one of the most used proteins in cell biology, letting researchers tag and watch molecules in living cells. It is sturdy, but slow folding can dim its glow when cells make it in large amounts.

The team ran laboratory evolution, selecting improved variants over generations, and used the secretory pathway's quality control to screen them. Their fast-folding GFP should light up more reliably in hard cases. Better folding reporters sharpen one of the basic tools of modern biology.
plos-pone-0002451:
Hatori joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Megumi Hatori, Hiep Le, Christopher Vollmers, among others. Its subject is inducible Ablation of Melanopsin-Expressing Retinal Ganglion Cells Reveals Their Central Role in Non-Image Forming Visual Responses.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002551:
Yu led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Kai Yu, Zhaoming Wang, Qizhai Li, among others. Its subject is population Substructure and Control Selection in Genome-Wide Association Studies. Determination of the relevance of both demanding classical epidemiologic criteria for control selection.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002651:
Leonardo de Oliveira Martins and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was phylogenetic detection of recombination with a bayesian prior on the distance between trees. Authorship is credited in the record to Leonardo de Oliveira Martins and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Genomic regions participating in recombination events may support distinct topologies, and phylogenetic analyses should incorporate this heterogeneity. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002751:
Caroline M. Nieberding and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the male sex pheromone of the butterfly bicyclus anynana : towards an evolutionary analysis. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Caroline M. Nieberding, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Female sex pheromones attracting mating partners over long distances are a major determinant of reproductive isolation and speciation in Lepidoptera. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002851:
Oluwarantimi Atijosan and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a national survey of musculoskeletal impairment in rwanda: prevalence, causes and service implications. The catalog record names Oluwarantimi Atijosan first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Accurate information on the prevalence and causes of musculoskeletal impairment (MSI) is lacking in low income countries. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002951:
Johann Pötzl, Catherine Botteron, Eugen Tausch and co-authors tracked a marked set of helper T cells after vaccination in 2008. Where T cells travel shapes what they can do, and the receptor CCR6 marks tissue-homing effector cells. Th17 cells are a helper type tied to defense at body surfaces.

The team traced functional, antigen-specific CCR6-positive Th17 cells following vaccination. Tracing means they could find cells aimed at the vaccine target, not just any Th17 cell. Published in PLOS ONE, the method helps vaccine scientists check whether a shot truly creates the cell type they intend.
plos-pone-0003051:
Ida Damgaard, Tina Jensen, Jørgen Petersen and co-authors ran a birth cohort study of undescended testis in Denmark and Finland from 1997 to 2001. In total, 2,496 boys were examined for congenital cryptorchidism at birth and again at three months. At birth, 128 boys had the condition against 2,368 healthy boys.

Risk factors were investigated prospectively, meaning data were gathered forward from pregnancy and birth. At three months, 33 cases remained among those checked. Published in PLOS ONE, a two-country cohort with exams at two ages gives unusually solid ground for judging which early factors matter. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003151:
Sara N. Vallerie, Masato Furuhashi, Raquel Fucho and colleagues ask where a key enzyme acts in insulin resistance in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme JNK1 is known to be essential to the development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. JNK also affects inflammatory signals, but it was unclear whether its action in macrophages drives fat tissue problems.

The title reports a predominant role for parenchymal JNK, the enzyme in the tissue cells themselves, in control of whole-body insulin sensitivity. Readers learn which cell types matter most for this pathway. That focus can sharpen where future diabetes drugs should aim.
plos-pone-0003251:
Jeanne Farrell, Lavoisier Ramos, Martin Tresguerres and colleagues resolve a puzzle about a knockout mouse in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mammalian soluble adenylyl cyclase, or sAC, is a source of the second messenger cAMP distinct from the widely studied transmembrane cyclases regulated by G proteins. Genetic deletion of exons two to four in the Sacy tm1Lex mouse was expected to remove the enzyme.

The title reports that somatic soluble adenylyl cyclase isoforms are unaffected in these knockout mice. Readers learn that alternative forms can survive a targeted deletion. That warning matters for anyone who interprets knockout results as total loss of a gene's products.
plos-pone-0003351:
M-J. S. Milloy, Thomas Kerr, Mark Tyndall and colleagues estimate lives saved by a supervised injection site in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Illicit drug overdose remains a leading cause of premature mortality in urban settings worldwide. The team sought to estimate number of deaths potentially averted by implementation of a medically supervised safer injection facility in Vancouver, Canada.

Readers get a modelled count of estimated drug overdose deaths averted by North America's first such facility. The study cannot count people who did not die directly, so modelling assumptions matter. Still, it gave policy debate a numeric estimate instead of anecdote alone.
plos-pone-0007451:
Dong Hoon Shin and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how tumor cells gain the ability to move. Spreading cancer must crawl through tissue, and an enzyme called MLCK drives much of that motion. MLCK is seen as a promising drug target for blocking invasion. The team studied a protein, Arrest Defective-1, that interacts with the enzyme.

They found that Arrest Defective-1 attaches an acetyl tag to MLCK. That chemical modification changes how tumor cells behave, including how they move. Controlling the tagging step could therefore slow cancer cell wandering. Slower wandering means less invasion and fewer metastases. The study points to a regulatory step that future drugs might exploit.
plos-pone-0007551:
Krisztina Johansen and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on blood chemistry in Parkinson's disease. Mutations in the LRRK2 gene are the most common known genetic cause of the disease. The team used metabolomic profiling, a broad scan of small molecules in blood plasma. They compared patients whose Parkinson's came from the LRRK2 G2019S mutation with patients whose disease had no known genetic cause.

The profiles revealed chemical signatures tied to each form of the disease. Shared patterns could serve both groups, while distinct ones mark the genetic form apart. Such biomarkers might aid diagnosis and help track how the disease progresses. They could also show whether treatments hit their targets. The study treats blood chemistry as a fingerprint of what is going wrong in the brain.
plos-pone-0007651:
Jennifer Taylor and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how skin builds its outer barrier. The epidermis renews itself constantly and faces a hostile environment. Its principal cell, the keratinocyte, matures as it moves outward, producing the proteins of the barrier. Those proteins protect against microbes and water loss. The team tracked gene expression as keratinocytes differentiate and form the barrier.

Genes switched on in coordinated clusters during the construction. The clustering is physical as well as dynamic: related genes sit together on the chromosomes. An organized program, not a scattered list, builds the front line of defense. Knowing the program helps explain barrier diseases like eczema. It also guides efforts to grow skin in the laboratory. The study reads the construction schedule of our most exposed organ.
plos-pone-0007751:
Eneour Puill-Stephan and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks for chimerism in a reef coral on the Great Barrier Reef. A chimera is a single body made of cells from two or more distinct individuals. The coral, Acropora millepora, spawns by broadcasting eggs and sperm into the sea.

Chimeras are known in at least nine major animal and plant groups. They seem common among sea creatures without backbones. The authors measured how much chimerism occurs in wild adult coral colonies. The answer affects how scientists think about coral growth, survival and reef recovery.
plos-pone-0007851:
Gordon King and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests how the plate a protein sits in can change crystal-growing trials. To read a protein's structure, labs first need good crystals of it. Screening means testing many conditions in parallel to find a promising start.

Screens usually run in ninety-six-well plates. The authors ask whether the plate's material itself interacts with the protein. Such an interaction could bias which conditions seem to work. Their results warn crystallographers that the plate is not a neutral bystander. Choosing plates with care may improve screening success.
plos-pone-0007951:
Laura Hughes and colleagues asked whether hunger early in life shapes bowel cancer risk, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dutch records let them track people who lived through famine as children or teens. Past work had linked lean early years to lower risk of this cancer in later life.

The team probed epigenetic marks, chemical tags on DNA that can last for years, as the likely bridge. Hard years during growth may set those tags in ways that change cancer risk decades on. The study joins a growing case that the body's early diet writes long-term notes on its genes.
plos-pone-0008051:
Heling Zhou and colleagues watched brain tumors in living mice drink in sugar, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer cells burn far more sugar than healthy cells. The team tagged a sugar look-alike with a dye that glows in near-infrared light, which passes through tissue fairly well.

Cameras tracked the glow as gliomas grown in the mouse brain took the sugar up in real time. Maps of that uptake could show surgeons where tumor ends and healthy brain begins. They could also show within days whether a drug is starving the tumor as hoped.
plos-pone-0008151:
Guy Madison built a sound illusion of a beat that speeds up forever in PLOS ONE in 2009. People are rare among animals in keeping time together by predicting beats rather than reacting to them. Music and dance rest on that forward-looking timing.

By stacking rhythms at several levels, the illusion makes tempo seem to rise without end, like a barber pole for the ears. No trick recording is speeding up; the brain's own prediction does it. Such illusions expose the rules the timing system follows, and where those rules can be fooled.
plos-pone-0008251:
Sigrid Marie Blom, Nicole Schmitt, and Henrik Sindal Jensen studied a drug-like compound in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kv7 potassium channels calm cells by reducing their excitability. They are attractive drug targets for epilepsy, migraine, and nerve pain. Those diseases involve cells that fire too easily. The compound studied here is an acrylamide known as (S)-2.

The team tested it on Kv7 channels expressed in frog eggs, a common lab setup. The compound acted as both a positive and a negative modulator, depending on the channel. Mixed effects matter when designing drugs for precise action. The study refines how this channel family can be targeted.
plos-pone-0008351:
M. Ruby Siddiqui and colleagues described leprosy program changes in Orissa, India, in PLOS ONE in 2009. India eliminated leprosy as a public health problem by December 2005. Elimination meant fewer than one case per ten thousand people. With that target reached, a separate vertical program seemed less needed. The national program therefore entered a second phase of decentralization.

Leprosy services were integrated into primary health care in Orissa. General health staff took over work once done by specialists. Integration keeps services available while cutting parallel structures. The experience shows how programs adapt after success.
plos-pone-0008451:
Jianbing Yan and co-authors mapped maize genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They used a new chip with many SNP markers, which are small changes in DNA code. Their sample held hundreds of inbred maize lines from around the world. Lines came from mild, tropical, and warm zones. Public breeding programs had supplied them.

The team found more than a thousand useful markers across the genome. They used them to sort lines by kinship and shared descent. They also measured how fast marker links fade with distance. Those measures help breeders pick parents and find genes for traits. The work gives a global view of maize diversity.
plos-pone-0008551:
Stacy Zamudio and co-authors study pregnancy at high altitude in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Living high up is known to reduce fetal growth. Babies born above a high threshold weigh less on average. Low oxygen to the placenta is thought to underlie this effect. Like problems occur in growth restriction and preeclampsia at any altitude. The team ask if low blood sugar also plays a role.

They propose hypoglycemia, or low glucose, helps cause the reduced growth. At altitude, mothers and fetuses handle sugar and oxygen in changed ways. Their data link low glucose to the origin of the growth drop. The work adds a metabolic piece to an oxygen story.
plos-pone-0008651:
Ivanka Savic and co-authors test a body odor in women in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Whether pheromone signaling exists in humans is still a matter of intense discussion. Androstenol is a steroid produced by the human body. It has been reported to affect human behavior. The team test if smelling androstenol elicits cerebral activation in women. They scan brains while subjects smell the compound and control odors.

They find androstenol activates the hypothalamus in women. The hypothalamus controls hormones, appetite, and sexual behavior. Activation there, rather than in smell areas alone, supports a pheromone-like effect. The work adds brain evidence to a long debate on human pheromones.
plos-pone-0008751:
Marcelo Golemba, Federico Di Lello, Fernando Bessone, and colleagues investigated a hepatitis C hotspot in Argentina. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Across Argentina, roughly two in a hundred people carry the virus. Certain small rural towns, though, show far higher rates. One such town stood out for genotype 1b, a viral subtype.

The team combined blood surveys with family-tree style analysis of the virus. Comparing viral sequences can show when an outbreak began. Their timeline points to how the infection spread locally. Such tracing helps health officials target screening where it counts most.
plos-pone-0008851:
Mojdeh Mohtashemi and L. Masae Kawamura looked for linked timing between TB and HIV among homeless people in San Francisco. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tuberculosis surged again in the mid-1980s in many countries. The rise is often blamed on the spread of HIV and AIDS. Among homeless people, the two diseases meet in crowded, hard conditions. Proof of true synchrony, though, needs data rather than assumption.

The authors compared the timing of TB cases with patterns among HIV-positive contacts. Waves of the two rose and fell together in their data. Synced timing supports a coupled epidemic on the streets. Outreach can plan for both diseases at once.
plos-pone-0008951:
Fredros Okumu and colleagues built and field-tested a fake human scent that draws mosquitoes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mosquitoes find people by smell, reading odours from breath, sweat, and skin. A lure that smells more human than a person could pull them into traps instead. The study ran outdoors where malaria-carrying mosquitoes hunt at night.

The team blended scent chemicals into a synthetic lure and set it against real human bait. Traps with the blend caught more mosquitoes than traps near actual people. A lure that beats the real thing can protect whole areas without using human volunteers. It also gives malaria control programmes a safer, standard tool for catching and counting mosquitoes.
plos-pone-0009051:
Basirudeen Kabeer and co-authors weighed three ways to diagnose active tuberculosis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Blood tests like QuantiFERON-TB Gold measure interferon gamma released by immune cells. A related marker, IP-10, rises on the same signal. The old tuberculin skin test is the third method compared.

Latent TB tests were already known; active disease in high-burden settings was the question. The team checked how each test performed where TB is common. Combinations might catch cases that single tests miss. Better diagnosis matters because active TB spreads while it goes unrecognised.
plos-pone-0009151:
Jean-Baptiste Rioux and co-authors found a second skeleton protein serving a bacterium's internal compass, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Magnetotactic bacteria swim along the lines of Earth's magnetic field. They build magnetosomes, small pockets that hold magnetic crystals inside the cell. The crystals line up along actin-like filaments to form a working compass needle.

MamK is the actin-like protein that threads those crystals into a line. The team found a second MamK-like protein in the species Magnetospirillum magneticum. Oddly, its gene sits outside the island of magnetosome genes. A spare compass builder hints at backup for the system, or a second job.
plos-pone-0009251:
Stefanie Beck and co-authors published this brain and motivation study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Working memory, holding facts in mind while using them, responds to motivation. But different kinds of reward may not act the same way. The study separated primary rewards, like food or money's basic pleasures, from secondary ones.

The team measured brain activity while people did working memory tasks under each incentive type. Primary and secondary rewards changed the dynamics of neural activity in different ways. Those dynamics track how control rises and falls across a task. Untangling reward types helps explain why motivation sharpens thinking on some days and not others.
plos-pone-0009351:
Nan Gao and co-authors published this eye defense study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flagellin, the protein of bacterial tails, is a loud alarm for surfaces like the cornea. It stirs strong protection against germs, chemicals, and even radiation. The team traced which signals carry that alarm in the eye.

Flagellin made the cornea produce antimicrobial peptides, small proteins that kill germs. It also sped wound repair there. The route they found is unusual: it needs the growth receptor EGFR but not the classic alarm switch NF-kappaB. A new pathway to protection could be harnessed to guard eyes after injury or surgery.
plos-pone-0011451:
Torsten Roepke and co-authors reported in 2010 that deleting one ion-channel helper gene in mice causes deep stomach disease. The gene, Kcne2, helps potassium channels work in many tissues, and its stomach role was not the expected headline. Mice lacking it developed a severe form of stomach inflammation with deep cysts, called gastritis cystica profunda.

On top of the inflammation, the mice developed stomach tumors. A humble channel helper thus guards the stomach lining against both chronic injury and cancer-like growth. The chain from one deleted gene to stomach disease was a surprise that reframes the gene's importance. For digestive research, the mouse becomes a new model of how stomach cancer can grow out of long-standing inflammation, and the channel pathway becomes a place to look for protective treatments.
plos-pone-0011551:
Maureen Durkin and co-authors examined in 2010 why autism diagnoses in the United States climb with family income. Autism spectrum disorder is recorded far more often in wealthy areas than in poor ones. That gradient could reflect biology, but it could also reflect access: wealthy families reach specialists who can make the diagnosis, while poor children with the same traits go uncounted.

In their cross-sectional study, the inequality in recorded prevalence pointed strongly toward diagnosis and service gaps rather than a true difference in how many children are affected. If counting depends on wealth, then prevalence maps are really access maps. The implication is practical and urgent: screening and evaluation must reach poor communities, or a generation of children will miss early help that wealthier children receive as a matter of course.
plos-pone-0011651:
Yann Hautier and co-authors measured seed death in a logged Bornean forest, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A classic idea holds that seed-eating animals help keep tropical forests diverse by thinning common seeds. Logging changes those animal communities, including the mix of small and large predators, which may alter that balance.

The team compared how predators of different body sizes affect seed mortality. Their results show size matters: large and small hunters do not simply substitute for each other. For forest managers, the lesson is that losing big seed predators can change which tree species return after logging.
plos-pone-0011751:
Pia Aravena and co-authors recorded brain signals tied to action words, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Past behaviour studies had shown a clear effect: grasping a sentence about an action interacts with doing that action at the same time. When the two clash, grasping the meaning suffers, which hints that language and movement share brain machinery.

The team measured the brain signature of this match-or-clash effect. Brain signals differed when the action in the sentence fit the reader's own hand state and when it fought it. That clash response gives hard proof that words stay closely tied to the body.
plos-pone-0011851:
Elizabeth Wilson, Jeremy Wong, and Paul Gribble mapped in 2010 how well people sense the position of their own arm without looking. This sense, proprioception, tells the brain where a hand rests in space. Few studies had charted how its accuracy changes from place to place across the area an arm can reach.

Their method tested position sense across a flat, two-dimensional workspace while avoiding active movement, which can add clues. The resulting map shows that the sense is not evenly sharp everywhere; some spots are judged better than others. A detailed map like this helps explain everyday reaching errors and can inform therapy for people whose position sense is damaged.
plos-pone-0011951:
Ki Sung Kang and co-workers reported in 2010 two possible benefits of the main active compound in green tea, known as EGCG. Levodopa, paired with carbidopa, is the standard symptom treatment for Parkinson's disease, and drugs that slow levodopa's breakdown extend its usefulness. In parallel, nerve cell loss in the hippocampus is part of the disease's wider damage.

In cell and animal studies, EGCG curbed the methylation that breaks levodopa down and protected hippocampal neurons from degeneration. One dietary compound touching both drug handling and neuron survival is unusual. The findings make a careful case for testing tea compounds alongside standard Parkinson's care rather than as folk substitutes.
plos-pone-0012051:
Hailun Wang and co-workers reported in 2010 a protein that moves when a tumor is hit by radiation, offering an early sign of whether treatment is working. Tumor response is usually judged by size changes on scans, which lag behind the real biology. Molecular imaging promised faster assessment of whether a regimen is helping.

The protein TIP-1 relocates onto the tumor cell's outer membrane after ionizing radiation, in proportion to response. A marker that appears on the surface is one imaging agents can reach. Reading radiation's effect within days, rather than waiting for shrinkage, could let doctors change course while change still helps.
plos-pone-0012151:
Camilla Benfield, Jon Lyall, and Laurence Tiley studied an antiviral protein in chickens for PLOS ONE in 2010. The Mx family of proteins fights viruses in many animals, switched on when the body senses infection, and some bird versions strongly resist flu. Reports on the chicken version conflicted: some said it resisted flu, others said it did not, and one clue was where in the cell the protein sits.

Their tests show the protein's place in the cell's main body is not what decides its weakness. That clears away a tidy but wrong explanation and sends the search toward other differences. For poultry farming, where flu outbreaks are costly, knowing why a natural defense fails is the first step to breeding or treating for stronger birds.
plos-pone-0012251:
William Halford, Ringo Püschel, and Brandon Rakowski tested a crippled herpes virus as a vaccine candidate in PLOS ONE in 2010. A mutant of the related herpes simplex virus 1, missing a gene called ICP0, cannot cause disease yet still teaches the immune system to protect against the normal virus. The question was whether the same trick works for virus type 2, the main cause of genital herpes.

Their mutant type 2 viruses proved unable to cause disease while still provoking immunity. A vaccine strain that is both harmless and instructive is the classic recipe for live vaccines. With no licensed genital herpes vaccine in existence, a candidate with this profile deserves the animal and safety testing that comes next.
plos-pone-0012351:
Victoria Lawson, Brooke Lumicisi, Jeremy Welton and co-authors studied prion misfolding in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Prion diseases, such as mad cow disease, spread when a normal protein folds into a harmful shape that resists breakdown. Sugary chains called glycosaminoglycans, found on cell surfaces, were already known to help prions spread, but the role of their sulfate tags was unclear.

The team seeded the misfolding of a mutant prion protein in the lab and changed the sulfate tags on those sugar chains. The level of sulphation altered how well the bad shape took hold and grew. The result hints that drugs which change these sugar tags might slow prion diseases, though much work remains.
plos-pone-0012451:
Mandeep Jassal, Gueno Nedeltchev, Jong-Hee Lee and colleagues tested a breath test for tuberculosis, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The idea uses a labeled, harmless form of urea: TB bacteria carry an enzyme that breaks urea down, releasing labeled gas that shows up in breath. A quick breath sample could thus reveal living TB germs at the clinic.

The team evaluated the labeled urea breath test as a point-of-care marker for diagnosis and for tracking treatment. A test that reads bacterial activity, not just DNA traces, could tell whether drugs are working within days. That speed matters most where TB is common and labs are scarce.
plos-pone-0012551:
Sandeep Kumar, Abhijit Sardesai, Debashree Basu and colleagues studied how a mycobacterial protein clasps DNA, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. HU is a small, basic, histone-like protein that packs the bacterial chromosome. Unlike its E. coli counterpart, the tuberculosis bacterium's version, HupB, carries an extra tail at its end, and that tail's purpose was in question.

The team showed the tail makes DNA binding more specific, tightening the protein's grip on chosen sequences. Specific packing helps the bacterium organize genes it needs in the host. Since HupB is essential and unlike human proteins, its gripping mechanism is a plausible drug target against tuberculosis.
plos-pone-0012751:
Fadok, Darvas, Dickerson and co-authors showed that lasting fear memories need dopamine in two brain areas. In fear conditioning, an animal learns that a sound or place predicts a shock. Dopamine is known to be essential for this learning in the startle version of the test.

Their 2010 study found long-term memory for the lesson fails without dopamine in the nucleus accumbens and the basolateral amygdala. Both areas must have it, not just one. That wiring matters for disorders of fear memory, such as post-traumatic stress.  The two areas handle reward and emotion in fear learning.
plos-pone-0012851:
VanDalen, Franklin, Mooers and co-authors tracked how bird flu spreads among wild mallards. Mallards are a main wild reservoir of avian influenza viruses. Those viruses pose an indirect threat to farm birds and, rarely, to people, so knowing mallard transmission matters.

Their 2010 study examined the routes by which the H4N6 flu type passes between mallards. Knowing the real routes tells surveillance teams where to sample and what to watch. Wild bird monitoring is cheap insurance compared with a poultry outbreak.  Their birds were followed through a full infection course.
pmc-10567551:
Sun, Chiou, Traylor, and co-authors report a large project mapping proteins in blood plasma for more than fifty thousand UK Biobank members. The work comes from the Pharma Proteomics Project, a shared effort by drug firms that compete in other settings. Blood proteins can reveal much about genes and health.

The team describes how the samples were measured and checked, both for sound technique and for real biology. They then share early lessons linking protein levels to genes and disease. A resource of this size lets many other teams hunt for drug targets and early warning signs in blood.
pmc-1636651:
Bedogni, Bellentani, Miglioli, and co-authors create the Fatty Liver Index, a simple score for predicting fatty liver. Fatty liver is the most common liver disease in Western countries, yet confirming it usually needs scans or biopsies. A cheap estimate from routine data could help find cases early.

Using data from the Dionysos Nutrition and Liver Study, the team built and tested their formula. They studied people with and without suspected liver disease in the general population. A simple, accurate score lets doctors flag likely cases and choose who needs closer checks.
pmc-2893951:
Kilkenny, Browne, Cuthill, and co-authors present the ARRIVE guidelines for reporting animal research. ARRIVE stands for Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments. The guidelines aim to improve how bioscience research involving animals is written up and shared.

Clear reporting covers how animals were chosen, housed, and assigned, and how results were analysed. Missing details waste animals and money when other labs cannot repeat a study. Journals and funders adopted ARRIVE as a checklist, making it a lever for more honest, reusable animal research worldwide.  Funders soon pointed grant applicants toward the checklist as expected good practice.
pmc-2973851:
Jombart, Devillard, and Balloux introduce discriminant analysis of principal components, a method for studying populations sorted by their genes. New sequencing tools offered unmatched power to reveal how natural groups are set out in space and time. The same tools produced data so large that analysis became daunting.

Older Bayesian grouping methods struggled with that scale. The new method combines two classic techniques to find and describe groups with ease, without heavy guesses. It lets researchers sort members into groups and see which gene traits separate them, aiding work from wildlife care to outbreak tracing.
pmc-3069751:
Murshudov, Skubak, Lebedev, and co-authors describe REFMAC5, a program for refining macromolecular crystal structures. Refinement is the stage where an atomic model is adjusted to fit diffraction data as closely and honestly as possible. REFMAC5 ships inside the CCP4 program suite.

The program uses different likelihood functions depending on whether the data are amplitudes or intensities, and on the problem at hand. Its components handle restraints that keep chemistry sensible while fitting data. REFMAC5 became a standard refinement engine behind many structures in the public archive.  Most deposited protein structures of its era passed through refinement of this kind.
pmc-4888851:
Selkoe and Hardy revisited the amyloid hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease in 2016, twenty-five years on. The hypothesis holds that disease starts when the brain makes amyloid beta faster than it can clear it away. Debate about it has continued for decades.

The authors argue that new lines of evidence from labs and clinics worldwide support the concept. They present amyloid build-up as a very early, often initiating factor in Alzheimer's. That view guides drug development aimed at clearing or blocking amyloid early. The review is a key statement in the long argument over what causes this common dementia.
pmc-5614451:
The GBD 2016 Risk Factors Collaborators published a comparative risk assessment in 2017. The study assesses, for the whole world, how much people are exposed to each risk and how much disease that exposure causes. The analysis covered a wide set of behavioral, environmental, occupational, and metabolic risks.

With estimates that run from 1990 to 2016, the study can track risk exposure trends over time. Critical exposures such as smoking, air pollution, high blood pressure, and poor diet are ranked by the harm they cause in each country. Tracking whether exposure rises or falls tells policy makers if prevention is working. The results guide where regulation and public health spending pay off most.
pmc-6943051:
Yuhao Chen and Xiaowei Wang described the miRDB database for microRNA targets in 2020. MicroRNAs guide gene silencing by binding target messages. Predicting those targets accurately is essential for understanding what each microRNA does.

miRDB predicts functional targets with a model trained on high-throughput experimental data. Users can search by microRNA or by gene and see ranked candidate pairings. The database covers several species and is freely available online. Wet-lab teams use the rankings to choose which predicted targets are worth testing first. Predictions can also be filtered by tissue, since many microRNA effects appear in only one organ.
pmc-7794651:
Kerstin Howe and colleagues argued in 2021 that human curation, careful checking by experts, remains essential for producing trustworthy genome assemblies. An assembly is the reconstructed full DNA sequence of an organism, and nearly all of biology builds on its accuracy. Sequencing machines and assembly software keep improving, yet error free assemblies remain out of reach.

The authors describe how expert curators inspect assemblies, spot joins that are wrong, break them, and repair the sequence. They show the scale of improvement this hands-on work delivers. Their case is a reminder that automation alone does not finish a genome, and that skilled human judgment still guards the quality of the reference sequences everyone else relies on.
plos-pone-0359951:
Gabriela Ghisi and a large international group of collaborators compared in 2026 how cardiac rehabilitation is delivered around the world. Cardiac rehabilitation helps heart patients recover and lowers their risk of further events, but many patients never receive it in a traditional center. The comparison draws on the 2025 global audit update of an international council for cardiovascular prevention and rehabilitation.

The authors contrast delivery through hybrid models, which mix center based and remote care, and through alternative settings, sorting the results by country income level and by decade. That sorting shows how newer delivery styles spread unevenly between rich and poorer countries. The audit gives health systems a benchmark for widening access to a proven but underused treatment.
plos-pone-0359651:
Emma Smith and co-authors explored in 2026 a way to read past stress from teeth, combining chemistry and visible marks. Teeth grow in layers, and the dentine inside records chemical traces of diet and stress as it forms, ring by ring. Separately, lines called linear enamel hypoplasia appear on the surface when growth is disrupted, often by illness or poor nutrition.

The team tests whether stable isotope trends measured along the dentine line up with those enamel defects, so the two records can confirm each other. Such work is aimed at skeletons from the past, where teeth may be the only surviving diary of a hard childhood. A validated method would sharpen how archaeologists reconstruct health in earlier communities.
plos-pone-0360251:
Madan Kumar Sharma and co-authors described in 2026 a sensor built for characterizing materials in mining, based on a microwave device called a CSRR, a complementary split ring resonator. Such sensors read a material's electrical properties from how it changes a microwave signal, without cutting or destroying the sample. Their design comes in dual versions and works at two scales, widening the range of materials and sample sizes it can handle.

Knowing a rock or ore sample's properties quickly helps mining engineers judge quality and guide processing. A sensor that works on site, rather than in a distant laboratory, can speed those decisions. The study contributes to a family of compact microwave sensors now spreading through industry and agriculture.
plos-pone-0356051:
Robabeh Emrouzi, Ali Janati, Masoumeh Gholizadeh, Mahmood Yousefi, and Sajjad Ahmadi published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns human resources professionals working in Iranian public hospitals. The authors set out to define what these staff actually do, in workload components and activity standards.

The framework is based on WISN, the World Health Organization method that matches staffing levels to real workload. Clear activity standards let managers judge whether a hospital has too few or enough non-clinical staff. Strengthening workforce planning for support roles matters because shortages there slow the whole hospital, a point planners across health systems can use.
plos-pone-0358251:
Nina Kemala Sari, Stepvia, and Muhana Fawwazy Ilyas published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns age-friendly cities, places designed so older people can live well and stay active. The authors validate an Indonesian version of a questionnaire that scores how age-friendly a city is.

Validation means checking that the translated questionnaire measures what it claims in its new setting. The study also compares scores across categories of Indonesian cities. Urban planners need a trusted local tool before they can judge which cities serve older residents well and which need changes, making this groundwork step important.
plos-pone-0360151:
Muloongo Sitali and two colleagues published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a review with a meta-analysis on embryo development in livestock species. The technique under study is co-culture with homologous oviductal epithelial cells, growing embryos alongside cells from the mother's own reproductive tract.

In vitro embryo production supports cattle breeding programs, and culture conditions decide how many embryos thrive. Pooling past experiments will show whether this natural-style co-culture truly helps development. Animal reproduction specialists and breeding companies are the readers waiting for the review this protocol sets out.
plos-pone-0359351:
Xiaoyang Zhang, Zhigang Xu, Songkai Liu, Bing Cai, Bo Deng, and Chao Kang wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on cable layout planning. It presents a hybrid method for the spatial layout of cables in complex equipment. One part handles interference obstacles with local post-insertion; the other uses improved Dubins curves, smooth paths first designed for vehicles.

Cables must thread through crowded machinery without clashing with obstacles or bending too sharply. A hybrid planner that fixes collisions locally and smooths paths globally suits that puzzle. Engineers designing wiring for aircraft, vehicles, and dense electronics are the audience for automated layout methods.
plos-pone-0358651: Stafford and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how people eat when smell and taste are damaged. The team looked at cross-sense effects, where sight, sound, or touch shape how food seems. Their early-stage work focuses on people who live with smell and taste disorders. Knowing how the other senses step in could help shape food advice and care for this group.
plos-pone-0358751: Mahula and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on maize lines that mature early. The lines are yellow and orange types, bred for food and feed. The team mapped their genetic diversity and how they group into families. Breeders use such maps to cross lines wisely, keeping diversity while chasing early harvests that dodge late-season drought.
plos-pone-0358851:
K C T Swamy and six colleagues simulate a technology meant to rescue weak millimeter wave links for future 6G networks, in PLOS ONE in 2026. These very high frequency signals carry huge amounts of data but fade fast and fail when walls or bodies block the direct path. A reconfigurable intelligent surface, a panel that reflects signals in controlled directions, can bounce a link around the obstacle instead.

The team built a realistic channel model that follows international mobile standards. It includes clustered signal paths and delay spread. They then ran a base station to panel to user setup at a common test frequency. An iterative algorithm tuned the panel's reflections to combine arriving signals as strongly as possible. Their evaluations compare the assisted link against a plain direct one to show where the panel earns its keep.
europmc-pmc8779751: Lopes and co-authors published this commentary in 2022 on peripheral nerve injury treatments and advances (new steps forward): one health (human-animal-environment health) perspective. It is an opinion piece grounded in the published evidence. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.

europmc-pmc8067651: A fresh look at Tax4Fun2: forecasting of habitat-specific working profiles and working redundancy based on 16S rrna gene sequences arrived with this 2020 research paper. Sequencing (reading DNA letter by letter) of 16S rrna genes has become a powerful technique to study germ communities. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.

europmc-pmc8037451: A fresh look at a comparative (side-by-side) review of natural and synthetic biopolymer composite scaffolds arrived with this 2021 review paper. europmc-pmc9178451: This 2022 review paper covers factors influencing adherence to mhealth apps for prevention (keeping illness away) or care of noncommunicable diseases: systematic review. Mobile health (mhealth) apps show vast in supporting patients and health care systems with the increasing. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.

europmc-pmc7124951: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on global telemedicine (remote doctor visits) implementation and integration within health systems to fight the COVID-19 pandemic: a call to action. europmc-pmc9113351: This 2022 research paper covers analysing high-throughput sequencing (reading DNA letter by letter) data in python with htseq 2-0. Summary htseq 2-0 provides a more extensive application (use) programming interface including a new representation for sparse genomic data, enhancements. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.

europmc-pmc7278251: A 2020 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at eating habits and lifestyle changes during COVID-19 lockdown: an Italian survey. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7384151: Doctors and scientists took on guidelines (official advice) for performing mendelian randomization (a gene-based test of cause and effect) investigations: update for summer 2023 in this 2019 research paper. europmc-pmc7055351: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on white matter disturbances in major depression: a coordinated analysis across 20 worldwide cohorts in the ENIGMA MDD working group. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7886651: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at revisiting the role of CD4+ t cells in cancer immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system)-new insights into old paradigms. europmc-pmc8118651: Doctors and scientists took on sex differences in biological (from living things) aging with a focus on human studies in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8314151: This 2021 research paper covers clinically applicable segmentation of head and neck anatomy for radiotherapy (radiation treatment): deep learning (layered computer learning) algorithm growth and validation study. europmc-pmc8205851: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at mdma-assisted therapy for severe PTSD: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled (against a dummy pill) phase 3 study. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9519451: A fresh look at a working selection shows previously undetected anti-phage defence systems in the E. coli pangenome arrived with this 2022 research paper. The ancient, ongoing coevolutionary battle between germs and their viruses, bacteriophages, has given rise to sophisticated immune systems including restriction-modification. europmc-pmc7241451: A fresh look at colistin and its role in the era of antibiotic (bacteria-killing drug) resistance: an extended review (2000-2019) arrived with this 2020 review paper. europmc-pmc7486751: A fresh look at IL-6 trans-cell-to-cell messaging triggers plasminogen activator blocker-1 from vascular endothelial cells in cytokine (immune signal) release syndrome arrived with this 2020 research paper. Cytokine (immune signal) release syndrome is a life-threatening complication induced by systemic inflammatory (swelling-related) replies to infections, including germs. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc7100151: A fresh look at the multidisciplinary team approach and quality of care arrived with this 2020 research paper. europmc-pmc9007451: A fresh look at Lipid21: complex lipid membrane simulations with amber arrived with this 2022 research paper. We extend the modular AMBER lipid force field to include anionic lipids, polyunsaturated fatty acid lipids, and sphingomyelin, allowing. king-henry-iv-part-1-pg2251: Eastcheap glows in this edition: Falstaff's tavern world of sack and jest stands against the cold honor of court and rebellion. Hal moves between them, biding his time until Shrewsbury. The greatest history play, rich with England's whole life.
john-halifax-gentleman-pg2351: Dinah Craik's 1856 novel about John Halifax, the orphan who becomes a gentleman by character. The Victorian ideal of self-help in fiction, beloved for decades. Honest, earnest, and deeply moving. The novel's moral earnestness made it a Victorian bible.
caught-in-the-net-pg2451: Émile Gaboriau's detective novel about a man caught in the net of circumstantial evidence. Methodical and ingenious, it shows the French master at work. This edition presents his classic in full. Gaboriau's plots are as intricate as spiderwebs and twice as strong.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume one of Casanova's memoirs: childhood in Venice. The great adventurer's beginnings, frankly told. Where the legend starts. First volume: a Venetian childhood, where the legend begins, a Venetian childhood frankly told, childhood in Venice frankly told.
plos-pone-0358051:
Elizabeth J Edwards leads a team of six reporting a careful null result on brain training for children, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The hope was attractive. A gamified program exercises inhibitory control, the mental brake pedal. It might lower emotional vulnerability in all children if delivered universally. It might even lift mathematics scores. Their preregistered trial randomized one hundred twenty-three Australian children aged eight to eleven to fifteen sessions of training or a control activity, with follow ups to three months.

The training did not transfer. Children showed no improvement on untrained measures of inhibitory control, and emotional and academic outcomes gained little, with a few trends favoring the control group. Benefits cannot flow from a skill that never grew. The authors question task calibration and dose in universal programs. For schools courted by vendors, this is the evidence that should slow a purchase.
plos-pone-0358951:
Beibei Zhang leads a team of eight sequencing two technologies to teach future preschool teachers how to watch children, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Observation is a core professional skill, but practice classrooms are scarce. Forty-six teacher candidates went through four workshops over six weeks that paired virtual simulation classrooms with authentic video of real settings. The researchers scored their observation assignments and interviewed them about the experience.

Each medium had its own strength. The simulation provoked more purposeful, active thinking, while real video sharpened attention to detail and to analysis. Across the sequence, analytical skill leapt and then plateaued, supportive commentary kept growing, and basic noticing held steady. Students described moving from confusion, through hunting for support, to reflecting on their own watching. The staged pairing, simulation first for thinking and video for finesse, is the authors' practical recipe.
plos-pone-0358451:
Wenyu Peng, Yuxia Sheng, and Ying Zhou present a deep learning method for predicting crop traits from DNA, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Breeders increasingly select plants by genome rather than waiting to grow them. But the bond between markers and traits bends in ways classical statistics handle poorly. Earlier neural networks also struggled, with vanishing signals and heavy computation. Their network runs convolutional filters in parallel rather than in sequence, and adds a coordinate attention step that weighs marker channels and positions jointly.

On four benchmark datasets, the method outperformed eight established rivals, spanning a traditional statistical model, three machine learning approaches, and four popular deep learning systems. The authors report the accuracy gains as significant across the board. For breeding programs, better genomic prediction means fewer field seasons wasted on plants whose genes already betray mediocre yield, quality, or resilience.
plos-pone-0357951:
Mireille Tuedom Chouegouong led a team of eight authors testing a plant extract pairing in rabbits, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The combined water extract joins guava leaves with Tithonia diversifolia, a plant known as Mexican sunflower. The team tested it in experimental rabbit colibacillosis, a gut infection caused by E. coli.

Chouegouong's results show the pairing improved metabolic balance and preserved the integrity of the intestine in this model. A treatment that protects the gut lining while calming metabolism is attractive where antibiotics face resistance. The work is preclinical, in rabbits, so human use is distant. Still, careful animal evidence is how traditional plant pairings earn, or fail, a path toward trials.
plos-pone-0355051:
Anna Stachel Kane and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on gluing together medical records and insurance claims without exposing patient identities, using tokenization, which swaps identifiers for encrypted tokens. The test case was hemophilia B, a rare bleeding disorder, where just under one hundred patients' records were linked and hand-checked, the small cohort allowing manual validation. The team judged linkage accuracy and how completely each source captured key facts.

Tokenization linked records with accuracy up to ninety-eight percent. Completeness split by source: the medical records held nearly all key clinical variables, while claims were patchier on clinical detail but carried the utilization and cost data records lack. Only a small share of medication and laboratory entries matched fully across both sources, underlining why combining them adds value. Tokenized linkage, they conclude, is feasible and reliable even in rare diseases, producing richer datasets for real-world evidence.
plos-pone-0357051:
Qiang Yue and coauthors published a 2026 materials paper in PLOS ONE on predicting the strength of grouting materials made from industrial solid waste. These alkali-activated blends are cheap and low-carbon, but their recipes are complicated and lab data are scarce, a hard setting for prediction. The team assembled strength records from three earlier studies, used a generative adversarial network to synthesize extra realistic training data, and tuned a gradient boosting model.

The synthetic data preserved the original data's statistical patterns and correlations, steadied training, and improved generalization to unseen mixes. The tuned model predicted strength with very high accuracy on the test set, clearly leading the alternatives tried. An explanation analysis then ranked the ingredients by influence, finding cement content among the strongest levers. The pairing of synthetic data with tuned machine learning, they argue, gives engineers a reliable design tool where experiments are expensive.
plos-pone-0357451:
Heavenlight Estomihi Masuki and coauthors published a 2026 surgical study in PLOS ONE on repairing full-thickness macular holes. The defect sits at the center of the retina and blurs straight-ahead vision. The work comes from two Tanzanian hospitals. The team reviewed just over one hundred operated eyes, tracking vision before and after surgery and whether the hole anatomically closed, then modeled which factors predicted success.

Vision improved by three months, gaining roughly two lines on the eye chart on average, and the hole closed in about seven of ten eyes. Eyes starting with better vision were far more likely to close, and closure tracked with real visual improvement. One technique, the conventional inner-layer flap, was linked to slightly worse final acuity in their modeling, treated cautiously given modest effect sizes. Results match respectable international benchmarks, they say, arguing for operating earlier, before vision deteriorates.
plos-pone-0354251:
Ghada Alturif and Wafaa Saleh examine how Saudi Arabia's decision to let women drive connects with women changing workplaces. The reform removed a major barrier to jobs under the kingdom's modernization plan, but hard evidence on career movement stayed scarce. The team surveyed close to nine hundred working women across regions and job types and modeled the odds of workplace moves against personal, household, and policy factors.

Holding a driving license stood among the strongest predictors of changing workplaces, alongside age, income, and marital status. Alturif and Saleh frame the result within a layered model of influences, from personal traits to national policy. Their findings support the view that mobility rights feed directly into women's career freedom, not just convenience.
plos-pone-0356551:
Zerihun Demessie Dilebo, Bekana Fekecha Hurissa, and Kebenesa Angasu Kitaba surveyed 260 nursing and midwifery teachers at four Ethiopian universities. The subject was the Objective Structured Clinical Examination. This is the station-by-station practical test used worldwide to judge clinical skills. Their 2026 study combined questionnaires with interviews. It gauged how well the exam is actually run in southern and central Ethiopia.

Fewer than half the teachers ran the exam well. Formal training in it roughly doubled the odds of good practice. A proper checklist and working equipment helped about as much. Negative attitudes halved the odds. Interviews blamed planning failures and shortages. Since weak exams can certify weak clinicians, the authors argue investment should start with teacher training and basic kit.
plos-pone-0355551:
Laura Ceballos and colleagues studied why a deworming drug, oxfendazole, kills liver flukes in sheep only at high doses, by tracing the drug from dose to blood to parasite. Their 2026 pharmacology study treated fluke-infected sheep at the standard worming dose or six times higher, then measured drug levels in plasma over time and inside the flukes themselves.

Blood exposure rose roughly fivefold at the high dose, and the flukes soaked up more than three times as much drug. That accumulation gap mirrors the drug's known jump in fluke-killing power at the higher dose. Liver fluke burdens livestock and people in many regions, so understanding the dose-to-parasite chain helps design treatments that actually reach the worm.
plos-pone-0352551:
Xiaolin Cao, Lianbin Xue, Fengxi Zhou, and Guoliang Dai ran indoor model tests on foundation piles driven into salty soil. Salty ground is common across arid regions. It quietly changes how buildings are supported. Their 2026 study loaded single piles and pile groups in layered saline soil at several salt levels. It built a matching calculation model. The model links salinity to the stiffness where pile meets soil.

Salt did not change the shape of how piles settle under load. But it changed the numbers in a welcome direction. Saltier soil settled less, stiffened the pile top, and raised ultimate capacity. Piles in groups interfered with each other, though the penalty faded as groups grew. The validated formulas give engineers a way to design honestly for saline ground.
plos-pone-0354151:
Wesley Colombo and four colleagues clean up the genetic naming system for leatherback sea turtles in this 2026 study. Leatherbacks migrate across whole oceans, and researchers track their populations using variants of one mitochondrial gene region. Over the years, studies used gene snippets of different lengths and named the same variants inconsistently, muddying the global picture. The team reviewed more than three hundred published sequences covering the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans.

They propose standard names tied to two fixed sequence lengths and catalog the known variants under each. Network analysis showed strong genetic structure, with one variant spread most widely. Reconstructed history points to a Pacific origin for the modern lineage several million years ago, with later spreads into the other oceans. A shared naming standard, they argue, will make conservation genetics comparable worldwide.
plos-pone-0355951:
Yang Xie and colleagues surveyed undergraduate nursing students in China about their attitudes toward palliative care, which supports patients near the end of life. Their cross-sectional study, published in 2026, asked how personal experiences shape those attitudes. The team surveyed several hundred students in late 2024 and early 2025 using a standard attitude scale.

Students overall held fairly positive views about caring for dying patients. Women and students with a seriously ill family member scored higher. Students in later years, those without hospital internships, and those who had lost someone close scored lower. So did students who had never received palliative care teaching. Xie and colleagues urge stronger death education, more clinical placements, and support for students who are grieving themselves.
plos-pone-0354751:
Qin Meng and colleagues designed a gene-silencing drug candidate for a serious fatty liver disease known as MASH. Animal models predict human responses poorly for this disease, slowing drug development. Their 2026 study paired careful chemical design of small interfering RNA with a human three-dimensional liver organoid model.

The lead molecule carried a sugar tag that steers it to liver cells and chemical tweaks that keep it stable. It survived well in human serum and liver preparations and showed few off-target risks. In the organoid model it lowered fat build-up and scarring signals, matching a drug already in clinical testing.
