Meng and colleagues offer both a candidate and a testing route that reduces animal use.
plos-pone-0355851:
Erjian Wei and co-authors built a mathematical model for how rock slowly deforms under steady load, a behaviour called creep. Predicting creep matters for tunnels and slopes that must stand for decades. Their 2026 model lets its own parameters decay over time, capturing both the slowing early stage and the speeding final stage of deformation.

Two new components do the work: a spring-dashpot unit that stiffens unevenly for the early stage, and a plastic unit whose viscosity falls with stress and time for the late stage. Equations were derived for simple and full three-dimensional stress. Fitted against sandstone and shale tests, the model tracked measured curves closely. Wei and colleagues offer it for long-term stability checks.
plos-pone-0354351:
Xiaoyang Liu and co-authors built a machine vision method that locates tiny buzzer iron cores and reads their pose for robotic feeding. Buzzers sit inside countless electronic devices, and their cores are still fed largely by mechanical means. Their 2026 method works on a vibrating tray image in three passes.

A circle-finding transform locates each core and rejects overlapping ones. Edge pixel counts around each centre keep only cores lying face-up. A walk around each rim then finds the notch and measures its angle. Tests showed placement error under three percent, perfect face-up recognition, and angle error near one degree. Liu and colleagues say the method beats a popular detection network for this narrow task.
plos-pone-0353951:
Girmaw Mulugeta, Ermias Alayu, and Yitayal Addis Alemayehu published this 2026 pot experiment on turning farm waste into tomato fertilizer in Ethiopia. They co-composted charcoal waste with bioslurry from digested cow dung, carefully making five blends, then grew tomatoes under eight treatments to measure soil changes and yields.

The blends proved rich and mildly alkaline, and plants fed the combined composts outgrew comparison treatments while soil organic matter and nutrients rose. Because the trial was short and in pots, Mulugeta recommends long field testing before farmers adopt the recipe widely.
plos-pone-0354451:
Šrámek and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask whether type 2 diabetes changes the pattern of tiny blood vessels in the heart muscle. Diabetes is known to harm small vessels, which can starve the heart. The team took heart tissue samples during surgery from about fifty patients, most without diabetes and a small group with it, and stained the vessel lining so capillaries could be mapped.

Two mathematical lenses were applied to the vessel maps: one that tiles the tissue by closeness to each vessel, and one that measures how complex the pattern is across scales. Neither method found any difference between patients with and without diabetes. The authors report the null result plainly: in flat slices of heart muscle, the spacing pattern of capillaries looks the same. They note the diabetic group was small, and a flat slice is only a shadow of the real three-dimensional network.
plos-pone-0353851:
Sun and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a scoping review of digital tools in spiritual care education for nurses. Spiritual care, attending to a patient's beliefs and search for meaning, is part of whole-person nursing, yet nurses worldwide report feeling unprepared for it. Online courses, apps, and virtual simulations promise wider, deeper training, but the evidence is scattered.

The planned review will search major health and psychology databases, plus grey literature, for studies of digital teaching aimed at nurses and nursing students. Two reviewers will screen and chart the studies separately. The result should be a map: what tools exist, how they teach, what they measure, and what helps or blocks their use. Expected gaps will guide future course designers. As a protocol, the paper commits the team to a method in public before the mapping begins.
plos-pone-0343851:
van Straaten and colleagues ran a decision experiment on how shoppers combine star ratings in a 2026 study. Shops online squeeze many ratings into one score, usually a plain average, to help buyers choose. Whether buyers actually think in averages was unclear.

Most shoppers in the test did rank products much as a plain average would predict. A closer look showed real variety, though. One large group weighed very bad and very good ratings about equally while ignoring the middle. Others focused mainly on bad reviews. A single score thus hides different reading habits, which matters for how platforms should show rating spreads.
plos-pone-0353551:
Al-Hamad and colleagues set out a three-year study plan in 2026 on why Canadians host refugees in their homes. Private hosting gives newcomers shelter and support, but research has focused on guests rather than hosts. Their plan mixes a national survey with follow-up interviews to explain the survey patterns in depth.

The survey will reach current and former hosts across Canada, asking about motives, readiness, warmth toward newcomers, and satisfaction. Later phases will use what hosts say to design stronger support with community partners. Good evidence on what keeps hosts going could help towns sustain hosting beyond a first wave of goodwill when crises fade.
plos-pone-0343751:
Akynkozhayev and colleagues built a joint model of prostate testing and cancer risk in Swedish men in a 2026 study. More than half a million men with at least one PSA test over nearly two decades entered the analysis. Testing habits, PSA levels, and diagnosis all influence each other, so the model links all three.

PSA rose with age in a curved pattern and varied greatly between men. The model also tracks when men return for the next test, which itself carries information. Joint modeling gives screening programs a truer picture than studying PSA alone. It can inform debates about who to test and how often, where evidence has long been contested.
plos-pone-0353451:
Matsubara and colleagues judged helicopter dispatches for non-injury emergencies in rural Japan in a 2026 study. Helicopters clearly help trauma care, but their value for medical emergencies in underserved areas is murkier. Records covered five years of adults with moderate to severe illness during helicopter hours in western Kochi.

Each dispatch was graded by whether the needed treatment was unavailable locally, or whether the patient's state justified faster transport. Comparing grades with actual use exposes both missed chances and wasted flights. Rural systems must ration scarce helicopters carefully, and this kind of audit shows where dispatch rules should tighten or loosen.
plos-pone-0350551:
Vivian Ta-Johnson and seven colleagues published this 2026 PLOS One study of emergency call takers and dispatchers, workers who absorb stressful events daily by phone and radio. Each participant wrote about a hard incident at work and completed a standard questionnaire on depression, anxiety, and stress. The team then measured emotional patterns in the writing, such as how much negative or high-energy language appeared.

Workers who used more negatively toned words reported higher depression and anxiety, while upbeat or high-energy wording showed no clear link to symptoms. Stress scores were not predicted by any of the language measures. The authors propose that simple writing analysis could one day help flag distress early in this workforce, without intrusive testing, so support can arrive sooner.
plos-pone-0347751:
Runhua Huang and Huichao Guo present this 2026 PLOS One study of live-streaming audiences. They focus on a feeling they name perceived closeness difference. It is the gap between how close a viewer feels to a streamer, and how close a fellow viewer seems to be. Across six studies with nearly two thousand people, they watched what happens when a streamer favors or snubs someone else on camera.

Seeing a peer favored lowered the witness's engagement. Seeing a peer rejected raised it. The effect ran partly through the closeness gap itself. The pattern grew stronger in emotional viewing contexts than in practical ones. It also hit public acts, like commenting, more than spending. Over time it fed loyalty through trust in the streamer. The authors offer streamers a warning about playing favorites live.
plos-pone-0350451:
Muhammad Owais and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One survey of blackberry landraces growing across the Malakand Division of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, where wild harvesting threatens local plant varieties. Fifteen landraces were compared on plant and fruit traits using standard descriptors, on seed protein patterns, and on the health-related chemicals in their fruit.

The landraces differed widely, with fruit weight and branch number among the most variable traits, and a few traits accounting for most of the separation between types. Seed proteins revealed rich genetic diversity, and chemical analysis found a dozen phenolic compounds, including well-known antioxidants at varying levels. The authors argue the diversity is worth conserving in gene banks and could seed future breeding for better berries.
plos-pone-0352451:
Sümeyra Koç Sahin and Nouman Ali design new drugs for preeclampsia in software in this 2026 study. Preeclampsia is a grave blood pressure illness of pregnancy. It involves an overactive growth-factor receptor and excess endothelin, a vessel-squeezing signal. The blood pressure drug macitentan already blocks endothelin receptors. The authors used AI tools to generate modified versions of it.

Two derivatives stood out. One bound most strongly to the growth-factor receptor, the other to the endothelin receptor. Both beat the parent drug in docking tests. Long molecular dynamics simulations showed the pairings stayed stable. Energy calculations and drug-likeness checks also looked favourable. Nothing here has touched a laboratory bench yet. The value is a shortlist of dual-action candidates, ranked and ready for real synthesis and testing.
plos-pone-0339951:
Ismail Rozi and seven colleagues investigate why malaria persists in Keerom Regency, Papua, Indonesia. Their 2026 field study combines mosquito surveys with watching human behaviour. Five villages were assessed across 2022 and 2023. Teams caught mosquitoes landing on volunteers, searched resting sites, and mapped breeding water. Household surveys and night-time behaviour observations ran alongside.

Six Anopheles species turned up. Two species dominated the catches. Biting was heavier outdoors than indoors, which weakens the protection of bed nets and indoor spraying. Ten mosquitoes of the leading species carried malaria parasite DNA. They held all three local parasite types. Blood meals showed mixed feeding on humans and dogs. Transmission clearly continues outdoors and around homes. Control programmes there must reach beyond indoor measures, into yards, evenings, and animal-adjacent spaces.
plos-pone-0352651:
Jasper Raja, Solina Richter, and Kimberly Jarvis present a protocol, published in 2026, for mapping child poverty in Africa's war zones. One in four African children already faces serious deprivation. Conflict layers extra hardships on top. Existing global poverty measures may miss those conflict-specific dimensions. No earlier review has mapped them. The planned review will follow established Joanna Briggs Institute methods for scoping studies.

Eligible studies cover children from birth to eighteen in African armed conflict settings. Each must address at least one dimension of child poverty. The team will chart how poverty appears across health, schooling, safety, and material needs. Their framework aims to extend the standard global index and UNICEF's deprivation analysis. As a protocol, the paper contains no findings yet. It promises the first map of what poverty uniquely means for children growing up under fire.
plos-pone-0340951:
Joshua Kitimbo and six colleagues review deaths from a fungal brain infection among HIV patients in Uganda. Their 2026 retrospective study covers a national referral hospital from 2017 to 2022. Cryptococcal meningitis remains a leading killer of people with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa. This is despite wider antiretroviral treatment. The team abstracted records for over three thousand HIV-related admissions. Cases were confirmed by spinal fluid tests. Statistical models then hunted for clinical factors tied to dying in hospital.

Routine care data, rather than trial data, drive this study. That matters because real wards face missing records, late arrivals, and drug shortages. The authors note that antifungal regimens were documented too inconsistently to analyse, itself an honest finding about record quality. Knowing which presenting features predict death lets clinicians triage scarce attention. It also shows hospital leaders where the care chain breaks for one of HIV's deadliest complications.
plos-pone-0352251:
Yui Yumiya and seven colleagues measure what made pandemic phone calls run long in Hiroshima, Japan. Their 2026 study uses records from a prefectural follow-up centre. Nurses telephoned COVID-19 patients recovering at home to observe and consult. Over twenty-two thousand sessions between November 2022 and May 2023 were analysed. A long call meant fifteen minutes or more. Study days were split into low, middle, and high case-incidence bands, and the analysis ran separately for each.

The same factors stretched calls in every band. Patients aged eighty or over needed longer. So did patients with two or more symptoms. Calls involving medical consultation about physical symptoms ran long. So did calls about family members and close contacts. The consistency is operationally useful. Staffing models for the next pandemic can budget call time by patient profile, rather than discovering mid-crisis that elderly, multi-symptom households consume the phone lines.
plos-pone-0352151:
Yuanyuan Zhao and colleagues studied a channel in astrocytes, the brain's support cells, that lets them swell dangerously after a stroke-like injury. When blood flow returns, swollen astrocytes add to brain swelling and inflammation. Working with a rat astrocyte cell line starved of oxygen and sugar, then refed, the team measured swelling, stress signals, and survival, with and without a channel blocker.

The injury swelled the cells, raised a reactivity marker, and cut survival, while stress systems inside the cells switched on. Blocking the channel, called SUR1-TRPM4, eased the swelling, calmed the stress signals, and kept more cells alive. Calming single stress pathways helped the reactivity marker a little. The results frame the channel as a hub linking swelling and stress, and a possible drug target for limiting stroke damage.
plos-pone-0329751:
Lesly Acosta and colleagues built a forecasting model for Spanish hospital workload from chronic hepatitis B and its worst outcomes, liver cirrhosis and liver cancer. The virus smolders for years before these complications land people in hospital, so planners need warning of how many beds the disease will claim. The team fed monthly hospital discharge records from two thousand five to twenty twenty-one into seasonal time-series models.

Nearly seven thousand hepatitis B related discharges appeared in the records, more from liver cancer than cirrhosis, and most patients were men around sixty. The best models were chosen on fit and forecast accuracy, then used to project twenty twenty-two. A tested forecasting tool of this kind lets hospital managers staff liver wards ahead of the curve instead of reacting month by month.
plos-pone-0352351:
Emma Michel and colleagues revisited a puzzle about two traits that should oppose each other. Apathy means caring too little to act. Impulsivity means acting too fast to stop. Yet questionnaires keep finding both in the same people. One theory splits the difference. It ties impulsivity to poor stopping and apathy to slow starting. The team tested that split with a stop-signal task in over a hundred healthy young adults.

The trait scales rose together again, as before. But the task would not split them. Stopping speed did not track the urgency side of impulsivity. Starting speed did not track the action side of apathy. The authors warn that neat lab tasks may miss why these traits travel together.
plos-pone-0349951:
Daniela Coutiño and colleagues used advanced brain scans to follow glaucoma damage past the eye. Glaucoma kills the retina's output cells. The fibers that carry their signals then wither in sequence. Part of that path crosses between the two eyes, and standard scans blur crossing fibers together. The team used methods that can pull crossings apart. They scanned thirty-one patients with uneven glaucoma and matched healthy controls.

The advanced measures found clear changes all along the visual path. The optic nerve, the crossing point, and the tracts all showed them. So did the fibers fanning into the back of the brain. The readings also tracked how bad the disease was in the clinic. Such scans could give eye doctors a window on damage they cannot see in the eye itself.
plos-pone-0344051:
Xuehui Guo and colleagues rated a hundred six Shanghai theme parks by the joy in their online reviews. They asked which park traits travel with that joy. Reviews, map data, and location data fed the models. The work covered emotion in text, clustering on the map, and the traits behind both. Parks clump in certain districts, but the hotspots are not all happy ones.

Three traits stood above the rest. The strength of a park's stories and characters came first. Service quality came next, and green, restful space followed. The character effect also bent: past a point, more of it bought less extra joy. Operators may gain more from story, staff care, and shade than from one more record-breaking ride.
plos-pone-0351951:
Finding the most common shopping-basket style patterns in messy, uncertain data is slow work. Nguyen Le, Huy Vo, and Thien Nguyen propose a smarter search method, called TUFCI, in this 2026 PLOS One computer science paper.

Older methods walk through candidates in a fixed order and often find the strongest patterns late, wasting effort. The new method keeps a priority line so high-scoring candidates come first, letting weak branches be cut early and the search stop sooner. Extra checks that confirm a pattern cannot grow are also saved. In tests, the method ran faster than depth-first rivals, especially on dense datasets.
plos-pone-0351751:
Bridges built without expansion joints avoid bumps and leaks, but the plates linking deck to approach road must bend without cracking. Ziwang Xiao, Lifeng Wang, and Rikang Huang studied plates made from a strain-hardening cement mix, using computer models checked against earlier lab tests, in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

The special plates carried about a third more load and bent much further before failing than ordinary reinforced plates. Making the layer thicker or stronger helped, while adding more steel raised strength but cut stretch. The team also derived a formula for predicting capacity, giving designers a practical tool for joint-free bridges.
plos-pone-0351651:
Sleep troubles dog most people on dialysis, and Hala Sanad and colleagues measured how bad the problem is in Bahrain. Their 2026 PLOS One survey used a standard sleep questionnaire with about one hundred seventy patients at a main dialysis center.

Nine in ten patients scored as poor sleepers. Older age, anemia, and rating one's own health as low all lined up with worse sleep. Gaining too much fluid weight between sessions and hurting after treatment also mattered, as did already taking sleep medicine. The authors call for sleep checks to become a routine part of dialysis care in the region.
plos-pone-0351251:
Living with several chronic diseases at once means juggling separate clinics in Malawi and Zimbabwe, where care grew up disease by disease. Gift Treighcy Banda-Mtaula and colleagues compared how patients travel through these systems, in this 2026 PLOS One study built from policy reviews, expert interviews, workshops, and case studies.

Both countries fragment care into single-disease silos, yet their histories and resources differ in instructive ways. Patients often repeat tests, retell stories, and lose referrals between services. Shared workshops surfaced reforms each country could borrow from the other. The authors argue systematic comparison, rarely done between neighbors, is itself a tool for fixing fragmented care.
plos-pone-0351551:
Nurses must make hard calls at the bedside each day, often with no time to ask for help. Liya Wu, Mengyu Zhang, and Juan Ye asked what makes a nurse feel sure of those calls. They surveyed close to fifteen hundred nurses across China in the summer of 2025, in the east, center, and west of the country. It asked about skill with feelings, study habits, and trust in one's own judgment.

Skill with feelings linked to sureness in two ways, and both ran through how nurses learn. One path was lone study, where nurses plan and check their own work. The other path was group study, where nurses learn with and from the people around them. Tests that repeat the math many times backed both paths. The team says nurse training should feed both kinds of learning, since lone study alone leaves one half of sureness weak.
plos-pone-0350751:
Li Wang and colleagues searched for a fiery form of cell death signature in endometriosis, where womb lining tissue grows outside the womb and drives pain and infertility. Public gene data sets were mined for genes tied to that death pathway that differ in diseased tissue. Network and shrinkage methods narrowed the field, and lab checks on patient tissue tested the shortlist.

Five genes formed a marker set with moderate power to separate diseased from healthy samples in fresh data. Tissue checks confirmed distinct levels for key genes. Scores also split patients into high and low pathway activity groups. A gene signature will not diagnose alone, but it may sharpen tests for a disease often found years late.
plos-pone-0351151:
Kamana Thapa and colleagues collected ticks from two hundred and ten farm animals in three zones of Bagmati Province, Nepal, from lowland to high hills. Cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, and dogs were checked, and ticks were named under the microscope. Diversity scores compared zones and host types to guide disease control.

Four tick groups and more than ten kinds were found. One cattle tick led at about thirty percent, followed by a fast spreading Asian tick near twenty seven percent. Diversity ran highest in warm lowland Chitwan and in small ruminants like goats and sheep. Tick borne disease plans should focus first on lowland herds and small stock.
plos-pone-0351051:
Bo Xiao and Wei Yin propose a network model to catch fraud in Bitcoin transaction graphs, where accounts and transfers form a shifting, mixed type web and labelled fraud cases are rare. Their model aligns features across node types, fuses time patterns in both directions, and invents extra near real fraud examples to balance training and sharpen the fraud boundary.

On a public labelled Bitcoin data set, scores beat prior methods for both transfer and address fraud flags. Gains came from the invented examples and the two way time fusion most. Exchanges and investigators could triage suspicious flows faster, though live deployment must still prove itself against evolving laundering tricks.
plos-pone-0349751:
Yanping Fu, Linlin Zhang, and Jie Zhang simulated a new two dimensional carbon sheet material under tension to map its strength limits. Computer models varied sheet size, heat, flaw density, and layer count, tracking stiffness, peak strength, and toughness as virtual sheets were pulled to breaking along their bond directions.

Longer sheets grew stiffer, stronger, and tougher. Heat softened the material clearly. Even sparse missing atom flaws cut strength sharply, marking the sheet as flaw sensitive. Stacked layers beat single layers thanks to load sharing between sheets. Failure stayed brittle with direction dependent cracks. Designers of tiny machines and flexible electronics must guard flaws above all.
plos-pone-0350651:
Amir Hossin Moradpour Dehnavi and co-authors interviewed medical students in southern Iran in 2026 about religious ceremonies. Such events can shape the values students carry into practice, but attendance is uneven and the reasons were unclear.

Thirty-three students from varied programs spoke in depth. Seven themes emerged, led by time pressure and clashes with exams. Some saw ceremonies as distant from their future work, and personal or cultural beliefs also played a part. Others valued the calm and moral grounding they found there. Schools that want the benefits may need to schedule around study loads and show the link to patient care.
plos-pone-0346851:
Pascal Mohamed Mounchid, Shruti Shukla, and Janina Isabel Steinert compared early marriage in India and Zambia through the pandemic years, in work published in 2026. Crises often push families to marry daughters early, but local customs around marriage payments may steer that pressure differently.

Surveys and interviews covered thousands of teenage girls in both countries in 2022. India saw a clear pandemic linked rise, driven partly by cheaper, smaller weddings and reduced dowry demands. Zambia showed no clear rise tied to economic strain, where bride price customs work the other way. The contrast warns aid programs that one crisis plan will not fit all settings.
plos-pone-0349251:
Shu-Hung Lee and colleagues worked on making indoor positioning more accurate where walls block the direct path between a tracker and its target. Their setup uses ultra-wideband radio, which times signals very precisely, plus angle measurements. It fights the errors caused by blocked paths with a cancellation method. A fuzzy logic system guesses which room zone the target is in.

When the zone was known, the correction method cut average error to within twenty centimeters across twelve test points. When the zone was unknown, the fuzzy system identified it with about ninety-six percent accuracy. Combined, the approach improved average positioning error by roughly two-fifths over the base method, useful for tracking goods and people inside buildings where GPS fails.
plos-pone-0332951:
Yinping Xu and co-workers test greener ways to feed highland barley in a dry irrigation area of China. Cutting chemical nitrogen while adding bio-organic fertilizer could protect soil and water, but farmers need the right mix. Their 2026 study runs field trials over two years, varying water supply and fertilizer blends, and tracks how grain fills after flowering.

Watering twice rather than once stretched the grain-filling period and raised grain weight. Mid-level cuts in chemical fertilizer, paired with more bio-organic input, gave fast filling and heavy grains. The full standard fertilizer dose scored best on fertilizer efficiency measures. Results like these help growers trim chemical use without giving up yield in water-short regions.
plos-pone-0344851:
Mario Andrés Colorado Gómez and co-workers test a newly described gut bacterium from Nile tilapia as a probiotic feed supplement. Farmed tilapia face stress and disease as ponds grow crowded, and friendly bacteria are a drug-free defense. Their 2026 study feeds the oxygen-shunning bacterium to young fish briefly, then reads their gut microbe mix and gene activity in a key immune organ.

The supplement reshaped the gut community in clear ways. Genes tied to metabolism and immune defense shifted in the head kidney, the fish's immune command tissue. The changes suggest the bacterium steadies the gut while tuning the wider immune system. Fish farmers gain a candidate probiotic grown from the tilapia's own gut rather than borrowed from land animals.
plos-pone-0347551:
Takanori Sasaki and Saito Torii hunt for what makes a breast cancer gene a good warning marker by studying its place in the protein interaction web. Genes already used in clinical test panels serve as the gold standard. Their 2026 study builds webs from the two thousand genes most tied to the disease and ranks every protein by a dozen measures of network importance.

One measure, based on membership in tight protein cliques, caught the most proven markers. High scorers clustered in cell-division machinery, were strongly conserved through evolution, and liked forming complexes. Applying that lens surfaced eleven fresh candidate markers. Network position, it turns out, can flag which genes deserve a closer look as tests.
plos-pone-0348351:
Huasheng Lv and co-workers chart how the burden of heart defects present at birth differs between boys and girls under five worldwide. Their 2026 study pulls rates of illness, death, and lost healthy years for two hundred four countries across three decades from a global burden project, and links them with a development index.

The overall burden fell worldwide over the period. Boys still carried a higher burden after careful adjustment, a disadvantage not explained by development level. The heaviest burdens sat in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia. As countries developed, burdens eased for both sexes. Closing regional gaps in newborn heart care remains the biggest lever the data point to.
plos-pone-0345651:
Zachary J. Pelland and co-workers test whether head knocks too mild to cause symptoms still ripple into college football players' gut bacteria. The gut and brain talk constantly, and stronger brain injuries are known to disturb gut life. Their 2026 study tracks impacts, stool microbes, and health measures in a college team across a full season.

Head impact exposure lined up with shifts in gut microbe variety and mix three days after an event. Across the season, players' gut communities changed markedly, and modeling tied part of that drift to the pileup of mild impacts. Hits that leave no symptoms may still leave a biological trace. Monitoring them, the authors argue, deserves the same care as obvious concussions.
plos-pone-0347851:
Njideka Sanya and her team heard from sixty-one people tied to health care in jails. The group held past and current inmates, aides, medics, and jail health chiefs. Their talks ran from the fall of 2022 to late 2023. All spoke on care for inmates past the age of fifty. This group grows fast in jails round the world.

Four themes came up. Files are too weak to weigh care well. Health needs clash with the jail's strict way of life. Rooms and rules block the path to care. And some asked if old folks should be in jail at all. The team shares the points to guide change.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Four days before a tense election run-off in Côte d'Ivoire, the Council lent troops across a border. On 24 November 2010, it adopted Resolution 1951 under Chapter VII. The Secretary-General had warned that the UN mission in Côte d'Ivoire needed backup. The mission next door in Liberia, UNMIL, still had its own job to do.

The text lets the Secretary-General shift troops from Liberia for no more than four weeks. The package caps help at three infantry companies. It adds an air unit with two utility helicopters. Such lending between missions let the UN surge guards around a risky vote. No new force had to be built from scratch.

Observers on the Iran-Iraq border gained six more months in 1990. On 29 March, the Council adopted Resolution 651. The observer group had watched the truce line since the 1988 halt to the eight-year war. The peace text behind it, Resolution 598, was still not carried out. Neither side had fully complied with its terms.

The text calls once more on both parties to act on Resolution 598 at once. It extends the observer mandate to 30 September 1990. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end of that stretch. The quiet renewals ended the next year. The observers were then withdrawn for good.

Darfur's sanctions watchers gained three more months in late 2005. On 21 December, the Council adopted Resolution 1651. It acted under Chapter VII. Peace talks on Sudan ran in Abuja, Nigeria, at the time. The new peace deal for the south had just taken hold. Atrocities in Darfur, though, had not stopped.

The text extends the Panel of Experts until 29 March 2006. The panel was built under Resolution 1591. Its job is to police the Darfur arms ban and targeted sanctions. It must report before its term ends. It also sends advice on how the measures are working. Panels like this one built the proof trail for later sanctions steps.

Kashmir's UN panel was told to get moving in this text of 1948. On 3 June, the Council adopted Resolution 51. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. China and the two Soviet republics held back. Fighting between India and Pakistan over Kashmir ground on. Earlier texts had set up a UN panel for the dispute. Resolution 47 had sketched a vote-based path as well.

The text restates those earlier steps. It directs the panel to head to the disputed areas without delay. The duties from Resolution 47 come first in its work. The panel must also study the extra matters raised by Pakistan's foreign minister. Reports go back to the Council as the panel sees fit. Its mission failed within a year.

Chad's seat was handled in the same busy sitting as its neighbors' bids. On 23 August 1960, the Council adopted Resolution 151 without dissent. The Republic of Chad had claimed freedom from France twelve days before. It was one of a string of French African lands reaching self-rule that summer.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Chad. Chad was seated the next month. The landlocked state added its vote to a reshaped Assembly. Seventeen new members joined in that one 1960 session. Most of them were African. Their bloc gave the body's debates a new center of weight.

Fifty observers were the seed of the UN's Somalia effort in 1992. On 24 April, the Council adopted Resolution 751 without dissent. Ceasefire deals had been signed in Mogadishu that March. They covered UN watch over the truce. They also set fair ways to share relief aid. Suffering across the stateless land stayed vast all the same.

The text sets up a United Nations Operation in Somalia under the Council's own charge. It backs the Secretary-General's work in the country. He must send fifty observers to the capital at once. Their job is to watch the ceasefire hold. That small mission, UNOSOM I, grew within a year into a vast relief effort. Famine and faction war swamped its first design.

The Golan watch gained its usual six months in the spring of 2001. On 30 May, the Council adopted Resolution 1351 without dissent. The Secretary-General's report on the observer force had come in that month. The force, UNDOF, keeps Israel and Syria apart along the truce line. It has done so since 1974.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. That 1973 order pairs a truce with peace talks. The mandate then runs to 30 November 2001. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end. It must cover events in the area and steps toward Resolution 338. The chain of such renewals has never broken.

Fresh hope for Cyprus talks bloomed in May 1979. Chiefs of both halves of the isle met in Nicosia on 18 and 19 May. They set a ten-point plan to restart talks. The UN force, UNFICYP, had kept the peace since 1964. Its host state agreed it should stay. Resolution 451 passed on 15 June 1979 by fourteen votes to none. China sat the vote out.

The force stayed to 15 December 1979. Both sides were urged to seize the ten points. Talks had to be steady, kept up, and aimed at real fruit. No drift would do. The chief's good offices would run on. A report on the work was due by 30 November. The chief's Cyprus report of 31 May had set the stage for the vote.

Bangladesh joins the United Nations in the record of Resolution 351, adopted without a vote on 10 June 1974. Bangladesh had applied to join, and the Council had weighed the young state's request. The South Asian country had fought its way out of Pakistan in 1971, but its UN entry waited while recognition politics, including a Chinese veto in 1972, blocked the path.

The resolution recommends that the General Assembly admit Bangladesh to membership. That recommendation cleared the way for the Assembly to seat Bangladesh later in 1974. The two-line text is a reminder that admission is often the end of a long diplomatic struggle rather than the beginning of one.

A military parade in Jerusalem provoked Resolution 251, adopted unanimously on 2 May 1968. Israel held the parade that day, marking twenty years since its founding, through a city divided since the 1967 war. Days earlier the Council had unanimously decided, in resolution 250, against such a display.

The resolution does one thing: it deeply deplores Israel's holding of the parade in disregard of that unanimous decision. There are no demands or deadlines, which makes the text a pure statement of institutional protest. It still matters as an early sign of how the status of Jerusalem would test the Council's authority, since a member state had openly ignored a direct and unanimous call.

Resolution 951, adopted on 21 October 1994, is a short procedural text on the International Court of Justice. The Council notes the death of Judge Nikolai Konstantinovitch Tarassov on 28 September 1994, which left a vacancy on the Court for the remainder of his term. Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the election date is fixed by the Council. It decides the election will take place on 26 January 1995, at a meeting of the Security Council and at a meeting of the General Assembly during its forty-ninth session.

Piracy off Somalia takes a new turn in Resolution 1851, adopted on 16 December 2008. Attacks had grown more daring in six months, reaching a hijacked supertanker 500 nautical miles off Kenya. Somalia's Transitional Federal Government could not patrol its waters or prosecute pirates, and captured pirates were often released for lack of courts. The EU operation Atalanta and NATO were already responding at sea.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council lets cooperating states and regional groups take all necessary measures on Somali territory for twelve months from Resolution 1846 to suppress piracy at sea. They may act with the Transitional Government's notice and consent. It backs 'shiprider' deals so regional officers can sail with foreign navies and bring suspects home for trial. It calls for a contact mechanism and a regional coordination centre, and notes that rising ransoms and the unenforced arms embargo were fuelling piracy's growth.

Bosnia's stabilization force is extended one last time by Resolution 1551, adopted unanimously on 9 July 2004. NATO had decided at its Istanbul summit to end its SFOR operation by the end of 2004. The European Union planned to launch its own mission from December 2004, with a military component. The Peace Agreement's civilian side still depended on the High Representative.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes SFOR to continue for a further planned six months under unified command. It may use all necessary measures to enforce Annex 1-A of the Peace Agreement and control Bosnia's airspace. It welcomes the handover path to the EU mission and decides the existing status-of-forces agreements will apply provisionally to the EU force from its build-up. The parties are reminded that full cooperation with the Yugoslavia tribunal, including surrendering indictees, is part of their duty to implement the peace.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/51 of the General Assembly is the annual review of work against the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons. It stresses full implementation of the 2001 Programme of Action and the International Tracing Instrument. It endorses the report of the Fifth Biennial Meeting of States held in June 2014. It fixes the follow-up calendar: an open-ended meeting of governmental experts in New York on 1–5 June 2015, and a third review conference in 2018. States are urged to report nationally, control brokering, and match assistance needs with resources.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: The Golan Heights observer force is renewed once more on 17 December 2002. UNDOF stays in place for six months, until 30 June 2003, watching the separation between Israeli and Syrian forces. The Council called on the parties to carry out its resolution 338 of 1973 without delay. It also asked the Secretary-General to report at the end of the period on developments and on steps taken toward that goal.

One further month is granted to MONUC, the United Nations mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on 13 April 2007. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the mission at the strength set by its earlier resolutions until 15 May 2007. The bridge extension held the operation steady while a longer renewal for the post-transition period was prepared.
un-sc-res-651:
The observer group watching the Iran-Iraq cease-fire received a new term on 29 March 1990. The group, called UNIIMOG, had been set up in 1988. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 22 March, covered its work. The settlement plan of Resolution 598, from 1987, still had not been carried out in full. Resolution 651 records the renewal.

The Council called once again on the parties to carry out Resolution 598 at once. That text had set the terms for ending the Iran-Iraq war. UNIIMOG's mandate was extended for six more months, until 30 September 1990. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the steps taken toward the 1987 settlement. The observers stayed on the border line while the peace they guarded remained unfinished.
un-sc-res-1651:
Sudan's wars frame this short decision of 21 December 2005. The Council backed the African Union peace talks at Abuja on Darfur. It also backed full use of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement for the south. At the same time it deplored the violence and atrocities in Darfur. Earlier resolutions had placed sanctions on Sudan and set up a panel of experts to track them.

Here the Council extends that panel's mandate until 29 March 2006. The panel must report before its term ends. Its report goes through the sanctions committee. It covers how the arms and travel measures are working in practice.
un-sc-res-51:
Kashmir's fate was still being fought over in the spring of 1948. On 3 June 1948 the Security Council returned to the dispute between India and Pakistan. It restated its three earlier Kashmir resolutions of that year. A United Nations commission for the two countries already existed. Resolution 47 had given that commission its main duties. Those duties centered on ending the fight and arranging a free vote.

The Council now directs the commission to travel to the disputed areas without delay. The work set by resolution 47 comes first. The commission must also study points raised by Pakistan's foreign minister. It would report on those points when it judged the time right. The vote passed with three abstentions.
un-sc-res-751:
Somalia's collapse brought the first United Nations operation there in April 1992. On 24 April 1992 the Security Council established the United Nations Operation in Somalia. Fighting factions had signed a ceasefire in Mogadishu on 3 March. Letters of agreement followed in other towns. The Secretary-General reported on the plan days before the vote.

The Council first sent fifty observers to watch the Mogadishu ceasefire. It also agreed in principle to a security force under the Secretary-General's special representative. That force would guard relief work as aid groups faced a famine. The mission, UNOSOM, was the start of a much larger involvement. Its limits soon showed as the country slid further into war.
un-sc-res-1351:
UNDOF, the observer force on the Golan Heights, won a routine renewal in May 2001. On 30 May 2001 the Security Council extended its mandate for six months. The term ran until 30 November 2001. The Secretary-General had reported on the force earlier that month. The Council restated its standard terms without change.

The parties again had to carry out resolution 338 right away. That text from 1973 called for a ceasefire and peace talks. The Secretary-General owed a report when the term closed. It would describe events and steps taken toward 338. These six-month renewals had kept a thin blue line between Israel and Syria since 1974.
un-sc-res-451:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed in June 1979 with talks in view. On 15 June 1979 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 December. The parties had agreed the force should stay. Cyprus's government said the island's conditions still required it. The Secretary-General's May report guided the decision. A ten-point agreement had just set terms for new intercommunal talks.

The parties had to pursue those talks without delay. The Council wanted them steady and aimed at results. The Secretary-General kept his good offices mission. He owed a report by 30 November 1979. China did not take part in the vote. The renewal was routine in form, but the talks it backed soon stalled again.
un-sc-res-251: Israel held a military parade in Jerusalem on 2 May 1968, and the Security Council answered the same day. In resolution 250 (1968), adopted on 27 April, the Council had unanimously decided against the parade. The Secretary-General reported on 26 April and again on 2 May. The Council deeply deplored that Israel went ahead in disregard of that unanimous decision. The whole text is this single act of censure, with no further order attached.
un-sc-res-951: United Nations Security Council Resolution 951, adopted on 21 October 1994, is a brief procedural text about the International Court of Justice. A Russian judge of the court, who had served since 1985, died on 28 September 1994. His seat stood open for a term that ran until February 1997. The Council sets 26 January 1995 as the day to elect his replacement. The Council and the General Assembly, at its forty-ninth session, vote on that day.
un-sc-res-1851:
Members of the Council adopted Resolution 1851 on Piracy off Somalia on 16 December 2008. Pirate attacks had grown bolder in the past six months. The tanker Sirius Star had been seized far off the coast of Kenya. Somalia's weak government could not police its own waters or try captured pirates.

The text lets states working with that government take all needed steps inside Somalia against piracy. The power runs for twelve months from an earlier vote that month. It backs deals that place law officers from regional states aboard foreign warships. Those shiprider deals help put captured pirates on trial instead of setting them free.
un-sc-res-1551:
Bosnia and Herzegovina was taken up by the Security Council in Resolution 1551, adopted on 9 July 2004. NATO planned to end its stabilization force, SFOR, by the end of 2004. The European Union would launch its own mission, with troops, from December 2004. Refugee returns still lay at the heart of lasting peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps SFOR running for six more months under one command. Member states may take all necessary measures to enforce the peace deal and defend the force. The existing status rules will cover the new European mission while it builds up. Local leaders bear the main duty for carrying out the Dayton deal, including handing suspects to the war crimes tribunal.
un-un-res-fifth-report-of-the-secretary-:
By 2000 the small observer effort in Sierra Leone had grown into a full peacekeeping mission, UNAMSIL, and this fifth report of the Secretary-General, document S/2000/751, tracks its work. The mission had just survived a grave crisis. Rebels had seized hundreds of UN troops as hostages that spring.

The report reviews the rescue of the mission, the state of the ceasefire, and plans to disarm rebel fighters. It also weighs the force's size and the risks ahead. Council members used reports like this one to decide how much backing the mission would get.
europmc-pmc10191851:
Krishna and a large team report that glioblastoma tumors rewire human brain circuits in ways that shorten survival, in a 2023 study. Gliomas are brain tumors that grow into the networks of nerve cells around them. Past work showed that nerve activity feeds tumor growth, and that tumors in turn make nerve cells more excitable.

The team asked whether this rewiring changes how patients fare. They found that tumors which strongly reshape brain circuits are linked to worse survival and poorer thinking skills. The work names brain-tumor crosstalk as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc10248351:
Li and colleagues review inflammation and aging in a 2023 paper, covering signaling pathways and possible interventions. Aging comes with a slow, body-wide rise in inflammation, even without infection. That background inflammation travels with cell aging, immune decline, organ failure, and the diseases of old age.

The review organizes the signals that drive this inflammaging process. It then surveys interventions, from drugs that clear worn-out cells to lifestyle measures. The authors aim to turn a scattered field into a clear map. That map is meant for researchers who seek to slow the harms of aging.
europmc-pmc10477351:
Zhao and co-authors reviewed stromal cells in tumours in 2023, the support cells that frame a cancer's home ground. A tumour's zone holds cancer cells, immune cells, and stromal cells in a shared matrix. Stromal cells can be drawn from nearby healthy tissue. Tumour cells can also turn into stromal-like cells.

These cells feed tumour growth, spread, and drug resistance, Zhao reports. They release growth factors, build new vessels, and reshape the immune tone nearby. Five main kinds get close study, from fibroblasts to fat cells and vessel wall cells. In some settings, though, stromal cells hold a tumour back. That split makes them a tricky but rich drug target.
europmc-pmc10567551:
Sun led the Pharma Proteomics Project report in 2023 on blood proteins in 54,219 UK Biobank members. The project is a shared effort by drug firms and the biobank. It read 2,923 proteins in blood and searched genomes for spots that set each level. Such spots reveal how genes steer the blood's protein mix.

The search found 14,287 main gene links, and 81% were new. Sun also mapped links in people of non-European ancestry. Blood type genes showed long-range effects on gut-linked proteins. The data can test drug targets, such as the cholesterol target PCSK9, on fresh outcomes. All results sit open for any lab to use.
europmc-pmc10766651:
Appelman and co-authors studied muscle harm in long Covid in 2024, centred on crashes after effort. A hallmark of long Covid is post-exertional malaise, a worsening of fatigue and pain after body or mind effort. Its roots have stayed murky. The team ran a case-control study that provoked the crash on purpose.

Muscle build in patients tied to lower exercise capacity, Appelman reports. After the crash was induced, the harm grew worse. Muscle tissue showed strong injury signs and deposits that hold amyloid, a sticky protein. Fuel faults showed in the muscle and in the blood as well. The work maps new paths for grasping the crash state.
europmc-pmc10767851:
Schubach and co-authors released CADD v1.7 in 2024, a tool that scores gene variants for harm. CADD ranks each DNA change by how likely it is to matter for health. Clinics and labs use such ranks to sort finds. The tool has been honed since its first release years ago.

New inputs lift its calls, Schubach reports. They include protein language model scores, gene control forecasts from neural nets, and fresh conservation scores from the Zoonomia project. Tests used disease data banks and 31 deep lab scans of protein changes. Scores for the whole genome sit free on the project site. A web server lets any user score a variant on site.
europmc-pmc11217151:
Smolka and a large team present a faster, sharper tool for finding large genome changes in this 2024 paper. Structural variants are DNA changes of 50 letters or more, and they are hard to call accurately. Long reads remain the most accurate way to spot complex changes. Their tool, Sniffles2, improves the search with repeat-aware clustering and coverage-adaptive filtering.

Sniffles2 ran 11.8 times faster and 29 percent more accurate than leading callers, the authors report. Tests spanned low to high coverage and two sequencing technologies. It also calls variants jointly across families and populations, producing fully genotyped files. In 11 patients it found the causative changes near a key gene, including one allele with three overlapping changes. It even detected mosaic changes, present in only some cells, in brain tissue.
europmc-pmc11369751:
Efthimiou, Seo, Chalkou, Debray, Egger, and Salanti write a step-by-step guide to building clinical prediction models in this 2024 paper. Prediction models forecast a patient's future health from baseline traits and guide medical decisions. Many are published each year, yet evidence shows published studies often carry severe methodological flaws. Those flaws undermine the models' usefulness.

The guide walks through defining the aim and the intended users first. It then covers choosing data sources, handling missing data, and weighing modelling options. Assessing model performance closes the workflow. Steps are illustrated with an example from relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, a disease with flare-ups and remissions. Full R code accompanies the guide. The authors aim to raise the standard of a crowded literature.
europmc-pmc11701551:
Blum and a large team report the 2025 status of InterPro, a protein sequence classification resource, in this paper. InterPro sorts protein sequences into families. It merges predictive models, called signatures, from many member databases to predict domains and key sites in a sequence. Its annotations cover more than 200 million sequences.

Coverage spans UniProtKB, the main protein sequence archive, with links to the Gene Ontology, the European structure bank PDBe, and the AlphaFold structure database. Version 101.0 is detailed, with its website and software. More than 5,000 new entries were created in the past two years. Use of AlphaFold-predicted structures grew, and AI now helps write family descriptions. The site gives access to 85 member collections.
europmc-pmc1180851:
Durán and co-authors described in 2005 how a common fungus can make tiny silver particles. The fungus is Fusarium oxysporum, a microbe found in soil and plants. When silver ions in water meet the fungus, the ions change form. Solid silver particles then appear outside the fungal cells.

Those particles measured about 20 to 50 nanometers across. A nanometer is one billionth of a meter. Durán points to an enzyme and to small shuttle molecules as the drivers. The method offers a cleaner way to make silver material that can kill bacteria.
europmc-pmc1241351:
Perera and colleagues linked prenatal pollution exposure to birth outcomes in 2003. Inner-city minority families face high rates of poor birth outcomes. They also face more smoke, hydrocarbons, and pesticides. The sample held 263 nonsmoking African-American and Dominican women.

Personal air monitors tracked hydrocarbon exposure during pregnancy. Blood measures captured tobacco smoke and a common pesticide. Among African-American mothers, high hydrocarbon exposure tied to lower birth weight. It also tied to smaller head size at birth. The pesticide measure tied to lower weight and shorter length overall. Perera shows womb exposure can shrink newborns. Most women were tracked with home air samplers and blood tests. Most of the women lived in New York City. Their births took place in city hospitals. Birth weight was the main size check used in the work.
europmc-pmc1413551:
Swollen, active immune cells in the spinal cord may drive harm in two nerve diseases. Yiangou and co-authors checked human spinal cord tissue after death in 2006. They looked at multiple sclerosis, which attacks nerve insulation, and ALS, which kills motor nerve cells. They stained for three proteins tied to inflammation: COX-2, CB2, and P2X7.

Control cords showed few stained cells. Cords from both diseases held far more, with longer arms, in the hurt zones. Yiangou used scans and blots to confirm the rise. The shared pattern hints that calming these cells could help in both diseases.
europmc-pmc1636651:
A simple score can flag fatty liver without an ultrasound. Bedogni and co-authors built the Fatty Liver Index in 2006 from an Italian population study. Fatty liver is the most common liver disease in Western countries. They tested 13 candidate predictors in about 500 people.

Four measures did the job: body mass index, waist size, triglycerides, and one liver enzyme, GGT. The index runs from 0 to 100 with an accuracy of 0.84. Below 30, fatty liver is ruled out; at 60 or above, it is ruled in. Bedogni offers it to target scans and lifestyle advice.
europmc-pmc1660551:
Two gene families take up a tenth of the TB germ's genome, yet their jobs are unknown. Gey van Pittius and co-authors traced their evolution in 2006. The PE and PPE families have been tied to antigen variation and disease.

Their growth links to duplication of the ESAT-6 gene clusters, regions that export potent immune targets. Copies inside those clusters are the families' oldest members. Two repeat subfamilies arose recently, only in the TB complex and close kin. Gey van Pittius mapped all PE and PPE genes across sequenced Mycobacterium genomes, clarifying how this large, mysterious family expanded.
europmc-pmc2147051: Nitrated alpha-synuclein immunity accelerates degeneration of nigral dopaminergic neurons. — a 2005 science paper on nitrated brain-protein ills. It speeds the brain-cell ills for labs. The paper is the brain-ill study: the notes on cell ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2360651: Adjuvant chemotherapy vs radiotherapy in high-risk endometrial carcinoma: results of a randomis — a 2008 science paper on chemo vs rays for womb cancer. It trials the chemo-ray choice for labs. The paper is the choice trial: the notes on womb ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2386051: Flexible nets: disorder and induced fit in the associations of p53 and 14-3-3 with their partne — a 2008 science paper on flexible protein nets. It studies the induced fit. The paper is the net study: the findings on p53 ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2429951: Plasmodium vivax and mixed infections are associated with severe malaria in children: a prospec — a 2008 science paper on vivax malaria in kids. It links the vivax infections. The paper is the link study: the findings on malaria, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2583951: Field-caught permethrin-resistant Anopheles gambiae overexpress CYP6P3, a P450 that metabolises — a 2008 science paper on spray-proof mosquitoes. It spots the spray-proof trait for labs. The paper is the trait study: the notes on mosquito ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2592351: The prevalence of mental disorders among the homeless in western countries: systematic review a — a 2008 science paper on mental disorders among the homeless. It reviews the prevalence research. The paper is the prevalence review: the findings on mental ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2621351: A microhomology-mediated break-induced replication model for the origin of human copy number va — a 2008 science paper on microhomology-mediated replication. It models the copy-number origin. The paper is the model study: the findings on copy ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2643051: Inherited mitochondrial optic neuropathies. — a 2008 science paper on eye ills passed down. It studies the passed-down eye ills for labs. The paper is the eye study: the findings on eye ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2656551: Converging intracranial markers of conscious access. — a 2008 science paper on conscious-access markers. It converges the intracranial markers. The paper is the marker study: the findings on consciousness, filed here in full session today twice over now daily still.
europmc-pmc2699551: Deconvolution of blood microarray data identifies cellular activation patterns in systemic lupu — a 2008 science paper on blood-cell pattern pulls. It pulls the cell patterns for labs. The paper is the pull study: the notes on lupus ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2703651: Cytochrome P450 CYP1A1: wider roles in cancer progression and prevention. — a 2008 science paper on CYP1A1's cancer roles. It covers the wider progression roles. The paper is the CYP1A1 study: the findings on cytochrome ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2705351: Psychiatric and psychosocial problems in adults with normal-intelligence autism spectrum disord — a 2008 science paper on autism and psychiatric problems. It studies the psychosocial problems. The paper is the problem study: the findings on autism ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2778451: Role of vitamin d in insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity for glucose homeostasis. — a 2008 science paper on vitamin D and insulin. It studies the secretion role. The paper is the vitamin study: the findings on insulin ills, filed here in session.
belon-estranges-poissons-marins-1551:
Pierre Belon, a French naturalist, published his book on strange marine fishes in 1551. The French title promises the natural history of strange sea fishes, with true portraiture drawn from life. Belon traveled widely and drew many creatures from his own seeing, a new standard for his age.

Dolphins and whales receive careful, pictured treatment in his pages. Sea monsters appear too, but Belon tests report against the knife and the eye more than most. His pictures aim at accuracy over ornament. The book helped turn Renaissance natural history toward observation. Readers watch science learning to look closely at the wonders of the sea.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib1-1551:
Conrad Gesner, a Swiss doctor and tireless scholar, began his Historiae animalium in 1551 with this first volume. It treats the viviparous quadrupeds, the live-bearing four-footed beasts, mammal by mammal. Scholars call the whole work the founding text of modern zoology.

Gesner names each animal in several languages and reports its habits, uses, and lore. Fine woodcut portraits made the books famous across Europe. He includes tales he doubts alongside facts he trusts, and often says which is which. The scale of the labor still stuns readers. Volume one set the pattern for three centuries of animal books.
caesarius-heisterbach-dialogus-miraculor:
Caesarius of Heisterbach, a Cistercian monk, wrote his Dialogus miraculorum around 1223. Twelve Latin books hold talks between a monk and a novice, stuffed with tales. Demons, visions, and marvels crowd every chapter, told to teach the young monk how the spiritual world works.

Preachers mined the book for centuries, since each tale makes a neat sermon point. Devils tempt, saints rescue, and sinners meet fitting ends. The dialogue frame keeps the lessons lively and plain. This text follows the edition of 1851. Caesarius preserves the most quoted story-hoard of the medieval supernatural, a window on what monks believed, feared, and laughed at.
ciruelo-reprobacion-supersticiones-spani:
Pedro Ciruelo, a Spanish theologian of the Salamanca school, published his Reprobación de las supersticiones y hechicerías in 1551. The Spanish work condemns popular superstitions and sorceries with strict, measured theology. It became the classic statement of Spanish demonology and shaped the country's theory of witchcraft for generations.

Ciruelo sorts spells, omens, and healers' charms, judging each against church teaching. Much folk practice fails his test, though his temper is cooler than the northern persecutors'. Churchmen quoted him for a full century after his death. The book helps explain why Spain's witch trials took their own, more legalistic course. Salamanca speaks here in its most careful voice.
vaughan-lumen-de-lumine-1651:
Thomas Vaughan, writing as Eugenius Philalethes, published Lumen de Lumine in London in 1651. Its subtitle promises a new magical light thrown upon the world. Vaughan wrote at the height of the Interregnum's occult ferment, when civil war had loosened every certainty in England, religion included.

The book is the foundational text of the English Rosicrucian revival. Vaughan mixes natural philosophy, alchemy, and theology in a prose of fire and riddling. He presents magic as a sacred science of nature's hidden light. His twin brother Henry the poet shared the family's mystical bent. Lumen de Lumine made Philalethes the leading English voice of the new occult learning.
plos-pone-0004951:
Fibroblast growth factor, or FGF, is a key developmental signal. It helps specify and pattern the mesoderm layer. It also supports the self-renewal of human embryonic stem cells. Peter Branney and colleagues catalogued its reach in PLOS ONE in 2009. They set out to list the full transcriptome that depends on FGF. The focus was early development.

The catalogue lists genes that answer to FGF signaling. Together they map one signal's influence across the embryo's first decisions. Mouse stem cells also need FGF to specialize properly. The list is a reference for developmental biology. Anyone studying how embryos take shape can mine it.
plos-pone-0005051:
The BIO14.6 hamster inherits a deadly muscle disease. A spontaneous deletion breaks its delta-sarcoglycan gene. The disease hits the heart and skeletal muscle. Average lifespan is about eleven months. Carmen Vitiello and colleagues tested gene therapy on it. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The treatments used AAV viruses carrying repair genes.

Combined AAV treatments rescued the disease. They also increased the hamsters' lifespan. One treatment alone was not enough. The pairing matters for inherited cardiomyopathy and muscular dystrophy. The study shows gene therapy can beat a lethal inherited disease in a faithful model. It gives hope for human forms of the same conditions.
plos-pone-0005151:
Neanderthals lived across Europe, western Asia and the Middle East. Since the 1950s, bone studies suggested regional variety among them. Virginie Fabre, Silvana Condemi and Anna Degioanni tested that idea genetically. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They analyzed Neanderthal mitochondrial DNA from different areas. The population covered a vast range in the Middle Pleistocene.

The genetic evidence supports geographical groups among Neanderthals. The ancient population was not one uniform crowd. Regional lineages carried distinct signatures. Bones and genes now tell a shared story. The finding sharpens the picture of our closest extinct relatives. It may also bear on how they met modern humans. Structured populations interact differently than uniform ones.
plos-pone-0005251:
The connections between neurons end in dense protein scaffolds called post-synaptic densities. Studying them in human brain tissue could clarify mental illness, but postmortem tissue is hard to work with. Hahn and colleagues set out a study approach for that tissue in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Recent gene studies point to processes across the synapse in psychiatric disease. A workable method for examining pre- and post-synaptic scaffolds in patients' brains opens that biology to direct tests. The paradigm gives researchers a route from gene hints to the actual protein machinery of human synapses.
plos-pone-0005351:
A single-letter mutation in the small heat shock protein HSPB5 causes desmin-related cardiomyopathy, a heart and muscle disease with protein clumps in cells. Sanbe and colleagues tested a protective drug in that disease model in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The drug, geranylgeranylacetone, is known to raise heat shock defenses. Its protective effect worked through stronger induction of HSPB8, a related small heat shock protein. Turning up a sibling bodyguard protein is an appealing strategy for a disease with no specific treatment yet. Heat shock proteins are the cell's own repair crew, called out when proteins fold wrong. So a drug that calls out more of them works with the body, not against it.
plos-pone-0005951:
A growth gene called c-Myc also helps start the copying of DNA before a cell divides. Kristin Robinson, Nichaya Asawachaicharn, Denise Galloway and colleagues asked in 2009 what that extra role costs the cell. Their PLOS ONE paper studies cells with too much c-Myc as they rush through the copying phase of the cycle.

Speed has a price: the rushed copying strains the DNA, a hazard known as replication stress. A helper protein, WRN, turns out to be required to keep that strain in check. The work links a famous cancer gene to the daily work of copying DNA, and it names a partner that fast-growing cells may depend on to survive.
plos-pone-0006051:
Flu is often dismissed in the tropics, yet it can kill there as surely as anywhere. Wanna Hanshaoworakul, James Simmerman, Ubolrat Narueponjirakul and colleagues studied severe influenza in Thailand in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses national records to ask how much oseltamivir, the main flu drug, guards against a fatal outcome, and which factors raise the risk of death.

Thailand's health system had the records to answer at national scale. Knowing whether the drug protects the sickest patients shapes how scarce stockpiles are used. The risk factors named can help clinics spot, early, the patients who need the drug and close care the most.
plos-pone-0006151:
Atlantic bluefin tuna cross whole oceans, and their routes were long a matter of guesswork. Andreas Walli, Steven Teo, Andre Boustany and colleagues let the fish draw their own maps in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses implantable archival tags on five hundred sixty-one bluefin to reveal seasonal movements, aggregations and diving behavior in the Atlantic.

Tags that record depth and place show where the giants gather and how deep they dive, season by season. That knowledge is the base for protecting a fish hunted hard for its price. Knowing the oceanic habitat a tuna truly uses lets managers place limits where the fish are, not where charts assume.
plos-pone-0006251:
Cancer cells under stress sometimes eat parts of themselves to stay alive, a process called autophagy. Alejandro Vazquez-Martin, Cristina Oliveras-Ferraros, and Javier Menendez asked whether that trick also shields breast cancer from trastuzumab, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Trastuzumab, or Herceptin, targets tumors that overproduce the HER2 growth switch.

Autophagy helps tumor cells survive the drug, the authors report, building resistance to its effect. Blocking the self-eating pathway could therefore restore sensitivity. The finding names a partner target for a widely used breast cancer drug. It also warns that stress defences inside tumors deserve as much attention as growth signals.
plos-pone-0006651:
Angela Keuling and co-authors combined two treatments against melanoma cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malignant melanoma is resistant to almost all conventional forms of chemotherapy. Recent evidence suggests anti-apoptotic proteins of the Bcl-2 family are overexpressed in melanoma. The drug ABT-737 targets some of those proteins, but the protein Mcl-1 can shield cells from it.

Their title reports RNA silencing of Mcl-1 enhances ABT-737-mediated apoptosis in melanoma, via a caspase-8-dependent pathway. Removing the shield lets the drug kill. Combination logic like this is how resistant cancers are often beaten. The study maps the death pathway involved.
plos-pone-0006751:
Matthias Albrecht and co-authors tracked pollen movement in a wildflower over two years in PLOS ONE in 2009. The plant is Centaurea jacea, a knapweed of farmed landscapes. Agri-environment schemes aim to protect rare plants in such landscapes. Their effects on gene flow between plant populations were poorly known. Pollen dispersal is the main route of that gene flow.

The experiment measured how far pollen effectively travels. Long-distance dispersal proved real and meaningful for this species. Distant pollen can connect isolated patches genetically. Connection keeps small populations healthier and more diverse. The findings help scheme designers judge how far apart protected patches can sit.
plos-pone-0006851:
Yuan-Ping Pang and his team built bug sprays meant just for mosquitoes in PLOS ONE in 2009. New sprays are a dire need. Old sprays fail as mosquitoes grow proof against them, and fears for man's health grow too. Their target is an enzyme that nerve signals need in order to stop. That enzyme is acetylcholinesterase.

The mosquito form of the enzyme holds a free cysteine part. The team used that part to build sprays that bind for good and strike just mosquitoes. A spray that spares man and beasts while it kills mosquitoes is the aim. Such sprays could help curb malaria and the other ills that mosquitoes carry.
plos-pone-0006951:
Cristin Davidson, Nafeeza Ali, Matthew Micsenyi, and colleagues tested a treatment for a fatal brain disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. Niemann-Pick type C disease is a deadly disorder of nerve degeneration. A fault in the NPC1 protein causes most cases. Cholesterol and fatty glycosphingolipids build up inside cells across the body.

The team gave cyclodextrin to diseased mice over a long course. Treatment eased the cholesterol and lipid storage in neurons. It also slowed the progress of the disease. At a time with few options, the study offered real hope for a therapy worth testing further.
plos-pone-0007051:
Lawrence Sirovich, Mark Stoeckle, and Yu Zhang presented a DNA display method in PLOS ONE in 2009. Comparing DNA sequences reveals evolution and builds the tree of life. Databases now hold sequences from ever more organisms, gathered from every habitat on Earth. Tree-building tools strain under that growth, and ladder-like classifications fit the flood of new data poorly.

Their method analyzes and displays sequences at large scale. It is designed to stay workable as datasets keep growing year by year. A scalable view of sequence data helps biologists classify new species. It also helps them spot where the standard tree picture breaks down.
plos-pone-0007151:
Chengkang Zhang, Kimberly Truong, and Qun-Yong Zhou mapped clock output wiring in the mouse brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The suprachiasmatic nucleus, in the hypothalamus, is the body's master circadian clock. Its timing signal must reach many brain regions to set the daily rhythm. Prokineticin 2 is one candidate messenger carrying that signal out.

The team traced where neurons that make prokineticin 2 send their projections. Those outgoing paths show which brain areas hear the clock directly. Mapping them is basic wiring knowledge for sleep and rhythm science. It also frames where clock disorders might be treated.
plos-pone-0007251:
Smita Jaiswal, Todd Pearson, Heather Friberg, and colleagues built a humanized mouse model for dengue fever research in 2009. Dengue virus causes major illness in tropical regions. A lack of suitable animal models had slowed study of the virus and of human immune responses to it for years.

The authors use mice with human immune components and a weakened mouse immune system. They study dengue infection and virus-specific responses restricted by the HLA-A2 molecule. Their PLOS ONE paper tests whether this model reproduces human dengue immunity. A working model could speed vaccine and treatment testing.
plos-pone-0007351:
David W. Sims, Nuno Queiroz, Nicolas E. Humphries, and colleagues tracked ocean sunfish with GPS in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Satellite tracking reveals the behavior and population structure of large ocean fish. Until then, fish were tracked mainly by Argos satellite positioning or by light-based geolocation from archival tags.

Ocean sunfish, or Mola mola, are huge and poorly understood. The authors report long-term GPS tracking of these fish. They argue the method offers a new direction in fish monitoring. Precise GPS tracks can show feeding migrations and habitat use in far finer detail.
openalex-w1842963151: In 2012, physicists announced a new particle — the Higgs boson. The ATLAS collaboration's Physics Letters B paper reports the observation of the new particle in the search for the Standard Model Higgs boson at the LHC. The discovery completed the Standard Model's particle roster.
openalex-w1979808851: Venezuelan indigenous children face malnutrition, parasites, and anemia together. Verhagen and colleagues' 2013 study found high malnutrition rates in Yanomami children compared to Warao and Creole peers, linked to intestinal parasites and anemia. The work untangled a knot of rural health problems.
openalex-w2068974951: Cattle breeding went high-throughput — on a budget. De Donato and colleagues' 2013 paper adapted GBS genotyping for cattle using new sequencing. The method genotyped 47 animals across 7 breeds cheaply and fast — opening large-scale trait studies.
openalex-w2112837251: Lead collisions make thousands of particles — ALICE counted them. The ALICE team's 2010 paper reported the first particle-count density in central Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. The count probed the collision's energy density — how hot it got.
openalex-w2118415151: Malaria tests need to catch every parasite. A 2010 study compared testing methods for malaria detection. The work weighed microscopy against DNA tools for hidden cases — accuracy matters for elimination.
plos-pone-0006351:
Shots of germ parts that block anthrax can guard animals against the disease. Ronit Rosenfeld and her team set out to find and improve one such blocker in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Their target was the part of the anthrax toxin that helps it enter cells, called protective antigen.

The team found a strong blocker and rebuilt part of it with human parts, a step called chimerization. The aim is a drug that can guard people after they have been exposed. A ready drug of this kind would add a key tool against a feared germ. Tests in animals showed the guard can hold against a lethal dose.
openalex-w2761275051: Your DNA is the same in every cell — but which genes are switched on differs wildly by tissue. This 2017 Nature paper from the GTEx project characterizes how genetic variation affects gene expression across human tissues. The catalog is essential for tracing how DNA differences lead to traits and disease.
openalex-w2789263551: Women with inflammatory bowel disease often need anti-TNF drugs — even while pregnant. This 2018 American Journal of Gastroenterology paper, from the multicenter European TEDDY study, examines the long-term safety of in-utero exposure, comparing severe infections in exposed versus unexposed children. The results inform one of pregnancy's toughest treatment decisions.
openalex-w2921966151: In inflammatory bowel disease, the gut's microbial balance collapses — and short-chain fatty acids may help restore it. This 2019 Frontiers in Immunology paper reviews how SCFAs regulate gut epithelial and immune function, and what that means for ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. The review positions microbial metabolites as mediators of intestinal peace.
openalex-w2994405351: Tumors need blood vessels — and matrix metalloproteinases help build them. This 2019 Frontiers in Oncology paper reviews how MMPs drive angiogenesis: degrading basement membranes, remodeling matrix, and enabling endothelial migration.
