The enzymes are accomplices in cancer's infrastructure project.
europmc-pmc2813751: Chemotherapy is usually seen as suppressing immunity, but this 2010 paper argues the opposite can happen. The authors show that pre-treatment with chemotherapy can make tumors more visible to the immune system, boosting adaptive immune responses against them. The finding supports combining chemo with immunotherapy. It reframed an old drug class as a possible immune ally.
europmc-pmc2876151: Cell division runs on a master switch called Cdk1. This 2010 review surveys the targets and processes under Cdk1 control, from DNA copying to cell splitting. The authors' overview maps the switch's vast reach. The review is a handy reference for the cell cycle's command center.
europmc-pmc2893951: Animal research reports were often too thin to trust. This 2010 paper delivers the ARRIVE guidelines for reporting animal research in full. The authors' checklist demands the details science needs to judge and repeat work. Their standards, widely adopted, lifted the field's openness.
europmc-pmc2910551: Fat tissue talks to the immune system, and the conversation can turn hostile. This 2010 review covers the role of adipose tissue and adipokines in obesity-linked inflammatory diseases. The authors' overview connects fat signals to illness. Their synthesis explains why obesity inflames.
europmc-pmc2920551: The shellfish poison saxitoxin has kin. This 2010 review covers nerve-harming alkaloids, saxitoxin and its look-alikes. The authors chart the clan's makeup. Their guide aids spotting tainted seafood. It pulls together chemistry, biology, and detection in one place. Shellfish farmers and food-safety labs both use it as a reference.
europmc-pmc2923151: Brains in conversation may sync up. This 2010 paper reports inter-brain synchronization during social interaction. The authors' dual recordings reveal coupled rhythms between partners. Their finding opened a window on the social brain. Later work used the same trick to study teamwork and empathy.
europmc-pmc2930851: White blood cells live fast and die young, and this 2010 review tracks them. The authors cover neutrophil kinetics in health and disease. Their overview follows the short, violent life of a front-line defender. The review aids reading immune counts.
europmc-pmc2973851: Sorting structured gene pools needs sharp math. This 2010 paper brings a new way to tell apart mixed groups from DNA data. The authors' method became a go-to for gene-pool studies. The work spread far and wide. Wildlife teams use it to track herds and schools.
europmc-pmc2976751: Rebuilding species trees from gene trees takes the right math. This 2010 paper offers a maximum pseudo-likelihood approach for estimating species trees under the coalescent model. The authors' fast method scales up. Their work aided big phylogenies. Thousands of species now slot into place.
europmc-pmc2990751: Tumor sorting can work from a single sample. This 2010 paper brings a simple template-matching method for sorting tumors with confidence scores. The author's method eases diagnosis. Their tool aided cancer typing. Clinics type tumors without big reference sets. The code is free for clinics to use.
europmc-pmc3004851: Smoking scrambles the airway's germs. This 2010 paper finds jumbled germ communities in smokers' upper airways. The authors' gene sequencing reveals the chaos. Their work links smoke to airway disease. Quitters' airways slowly regain healthy germs. The chaos may seed chronic lung infections.
europmc-pmc3069751: Crystal structures got a refiner. This 2011 paper covers REFMAC5, the workhorse for polishing crystal structures. The authors' program became a lab standard. Their software shaped structural biology. Every deposited structure likely passed through it. The refiner squeezes signal from noise.
europmc-pmc3082551: Aging rats run low on NAD+ and Sirt1. This 2011 paper tracks falling NAD+, rising oxidant stress, and fading Sirt1 in aging rats. The authors chart the decline. Their work backs NAD+ boosters. Old organs showed the steepest drops. Supplement sellers cite the study widely.
europmc-pmc3094351: A lifetime of inflammation shortens chromosome caps. This 2011 study ties piled-up inflammation to shorter telomeres in older adults. The authors bridge inflammation and aging. Their work backs anti-inflammatory living. Exercise and sleep slowed the shortening. The effect rivaled smoking's toll.
europmc-pmc3118151: Hip fractures kill one in three elders. This 2011 population study tracks mortality and causes of death after hip fracture in seniors. The authors reveal the grim toll. Their work drives prevention. Heart failure led the causes. Fast surgery cut the death rate.
europmc-pmc3121651: An old malaria drug got a modern review. This 2011 paper covers quinine's role in treating malaria today. The authors weigh its place. Their overview guides clinicians. It remains the fallback for severe cases. Newer drugs beat it on tolerability. The review spans centuries of use.
europmc-pmc3127851: Asia-Pacific malaria mosquitoes got mapped. This 2011 paper maps dominant Anopheles vectors with occurrence data and bionomic notes. The authors' maps guide control. Their work aids elimination. Forty-one vector species made the maps. Spray teams plan routes from them. The atlas underpins regional strategy.
europmc-pmc3138751: Severe burns scar the body for years. This 2011 paper shows the body's stress response to burns persists long-term. The authors track the lingering damage. Their work guides rehab. Metabolism stayed revved for years. Exercise programs now run for the long haul.
europmc-pmc3141051: Tiny antibiotic doses breed resistance. This 2011 paper shows even very low antibiotic levels select resistant bacteria. The authors reveal the hidden driver. Their work shaped stewardship. Farm runoff carried enough to select. The finding tightened discharge rules. Hospitals audit their waste streams.
europmc-pmc3203851: Drug hunting got a simulation review. This 2011 paper reviews computer simulations of molecules in drug design. The authors survey the methods. Their overview guides designers. Simulations now run on gaming chips. The review trained a generation. It is a citation giant.
europmc-pmc3237351: Diesel exhaust primed brain immune cells. This 2011 paper shows diesel fumes activate microglia and worsen dopamine damage. The authors reveal the priming. Qin-Yi Zhang and eight co-authors build a learn solver for systems where a fluid and a solid move each other. A wing bends in wind, and its bend shifts the wind. Their solver is called HGATSolver. It uses a mixed graph focus net, with nodes for fluid and solid in one graph. Focus weights let each side keep its own voice at the meet face. A reader in sim work gets a fast solver that still hears the split of the pair.

Their 2026 arXiv paper gives a perturbative, non-Markovian treatment of low-temperature spin decoherence. Molecular spins are promising carriers for quantum sensing and computing.

Their coherence is eroded by nuclear spins in the molecule and its surroundings. At low temperatures the bath has memory, so Markovian models miss the physics. The authors build a treatment that keeps that memory while staying tractable. Better decoherence models can help chemists design molecules that hold their quantum states longer.

The team work out the Kerr and Faraday effects in the microwave range. Light that hits the stuff twists as it bounces or passes. They show the clapping modes sit well below the gap for loose parts. In multi band cases, those modes rule the twist reply. The work gives a new probe of the order in such stuffs.

Past maps work for still, plain, Hermitian rigs. The team grow it to rigs that leak, blink in time, or have edge states. They build the map from the product of the law and its dual. The map keeps its shape sense in the new cases. It can now guide work on a far wider set of rigs.
arxiv-2601-10651:
Christoph Weinhuber, Yannik Schnitzer, Alessandro Abate, David Parker, Giuseppe De Giacomo, and Moshe Y. Vardi study synthesis with many properties at once. Synthesis means building a system that is sure to meet a stated goal. The goals here are written in LTLf, a logic for finite runs. The catch is that meeting all goals at once may be impossible.

Rather than test subsets of goals one by one, they compute in a single fixed-point pass. The pass links each game state to the sets of goals that can still be won from it. They then build strategies that achieve the largest winnable sets. The result helps designers of reactive systems get the most from conflicting demands.
arxiv-2601-10751:
Diego Linares and Carlos Cadenas explore the dynamics of a modified Chebyshev root-finding method. Root-finding methods chase the zeros of a function by iteration. When roots repeat, the standard tools slow or fail, so variants for multiple roots exist. Each method traces a rational function whose orbits decide success or chaos.

The authors set out the base theory of discrete dynamical systems, then track the method's behavior. They classify the stability of its fixed points and follow its critical orbits. Stable points draw iterations in; unstable ones fling them away. The map tells users where the method can be trusted and where it may wander.
arxiv-2601-11151:
Ji Dai and co-authors present a cross-modal attention network with dual graph learning for multimodal recommendation. Multimedia recommenders use user-item interactions plus images, text, and other modes. Past methods often fuse modes by simple concatenation, a shallow blend. They also treat users thinly, building rich item profiles but weak user profiles.

The authors attack both limits. Cross-modal attention lets modes inform each other deeply. Dual graph learning models users and items with matching care. Richer fusion and symmetric treatment aim at recommendations that fit taste more closely. The work serves streaming and shopping platforms where a poster, a blurb, and a history must jointly predict what a user wants next.
arxiv-2601-12251:
Zejing Zhang, Jun Meng, Zhongpu Qiu, and a large team forecast the El Niño-Southern Oscillation over long leads with a physics-guided network. ENSO is a top mode of year-to-year climate swings. What caps its long-lead forecast skill is still unclear.

Their Deep Echo State Network runs on climate modes picked from the extended recharge oscillator frame. Those modes have clear physical sense. They report skillful forecasts for the Niño 3 index. A physics-led model could stretch warning times for floods and droughts.  Long leads give more time to plan for dry spells.
arxiv-2601-11351:
Ruifeng Zheng and six coauthors model a receiver that talks in molecules. Their 2026 preprint deals with microfluidic molecular communication. Signals here are puffs of molecules in tiny channels. The receiver binds them by Langmuir adsorption on a surface.

The surface has finite room, so it can fill and saturate. The team works in the regime where reactions set the pace. They derive a clean form for the single-pulse response. They also give a recursion for on-off keying at symbol rate. The math shows the channel's memory in plain terms. It also shows inter-symbol interference, where past symbols blur new ones. Such models help design links for chips and medical micro-devices.
arxiv-2601-11451:
Oishee Bintey Hoque and six coauthors map large livestock farms from orbit. Their 2026 preprint is named PRISM-CAFO, on remote-sensing segmentation. CAFOs are concentrated animal feeding operations, vast by design. They pose real risks to health and to the environment.

Such farms are also at risk from disease and extreme weather. Their count keeps growing across the United States. Sound, scalable maps of them are more needed than ever. The team's tool segments satellite imagery to find CAFO sites. Prior knowledge conditions the segmentation for better accuracy. Good maps help agencies watch risks and plan responses. The work serves public health as much as land policy.
arxiv-2601-11551:
Masoud Gharahi releases code that reads ranks of multipartite quantum states. The 2026 preprint presents a Mathematica codebase for the task. The target quantity is the l-multilinear rank, or multirank. Tensor flattening is the technique at the codebase's core.

Flattening turns a tensor into matrices along each split. The ranks of all bipartition-induced matrices are then computed. Those ranks give a criterion for a prized trait. The trait is genuine multipartite entanglement in the state. Systems hold qudits, units with local dimension d each. A ready codebase saves labs from coding the test by hand. It also makes results easier to check and repeat.
arxiv-2601-11651:
Miriam Doh, Aditya Gulati, Corinna Canali, and Nuria Oliver expose algorithmic lookism. Their 2026 preprint studies bias tied to physical appearance. Text-to-image models can favor attractive faces systematically. A downstream gender classification task is also tested.

The team analyzed 26,400 synthetic faces for the study. Stable Diffusion 2.1 and 3.5 Medium made the faces. Generative models link attractiveness with positive attributes. They link plain looks with negative ones in mirror form. Those links mirror socially built biases, not evidence. The paper frames the pattern as structural harm. Audits of this kind press for fairer generative systems.
arxiv-2601-13051:
Ankit Kumar, Hermenegildo Borges de Oliveira, and Manil T. Mohan study a thick fluid flow law. The law is a broad form of the Navier-Stokes-Voigt set, a model that adds a stiff spring like term to the classic flow laws. The flow cannot be squeezed, and it sits in a bounded zone.

The team asks when weak answers to the law can be said to exist in the best way. Weak answers are the loose kind used when smooth answers may fail. Their zone may have two dims or more. Such proofs set the base for all later work on how the fluid moves, how long answers last, and how code can track them. The paper adds care to a model used for thick and slow flows.
arxiv-2601-13251:
Ebubekir Tosun, Mehmet Emin Buldur, Ozay Ezerceli, and Mahmoud ElHussieni tackle a blind spot in word embeddings. Such maps place words by how they act in text. They are poor at one split, though. True kin words and their foes, antonyms, can land close in the map.

Just raising the bar for how close words must be fails to keep foes out. The team built a huge graph of Turkish synonym links to face that flaw head on. The graph holds 15 million nodes. Their cluster method is made to split kin from foes as it groups. For Turkish language tools, the work fills a gap that English first methods left wide open.
arxiv-2601-13351:
Rute C. Sofia and a large team federate container fleets past the cloud core. Their frame is called CODECO. It grows Kubernetes, the stock tool to run container apps, for use across split sites and firms. Cloud first set ups strain when gear is spread, mobile, or owned by many hands.

CODECO joins data, compute, and net picks in one act, a co orchestration. It adds sense rich app forms, a split by parts form of federation, and AI aid for picks. Apps and their micro parts can then be placed and run with the local state in mind. For edge and multi firm teams, the frame fits a world the cloud core was not built for.
arxiv-2601-13551:
Feng Ding and co-authors built a face data set to test deepfake tools on fine local fakes. AI face tools now make fakes too fine to catch by eye. That skill is a privacy risk. Old fake face sets skip fine local edits, where just one face zone is swapped.

They also skip splice attacks, fakes made by join of real and fake parts. Such joins can fool a detector in a way a full fake does not. The team calls those cases detector evasive samples. Their set is built to hold them. For detector teams, a set that holds the hard case is worth more than a big set of easy fakes.
arxiv-2601-12451:
Sam Adriaensen proves a result in finite projective geometry. The objects are even sets in the space PG of dimension n over a finite field. An even set meets every line in an even number of points. The question is what the smallest such sets look like. Small extremal objects often have a rigid, clean shape.

Adriaensen shows that the smallest even sets are cylinders. The base of each cylinder is a hyperoval, a known rich shape in plane geometry. The result sits inside a broader study of dual projective geometric codes. Codes and geometry inform each other here. A clean form for the smallest sets helps pin down traits of those codes as well.
arxiv-2601-12751:
Manjish Pal puts forward a new way to judge what graph neural networks can and cannot tell apart. These networks learn from data shaped as graphs, with nodes and links. A key test is which graph traits a network can pick up at all. Pal bases his frame on the theory of Boolean functions, the math of true and false values.

He brings in a new marker for this test. The marker tracks how a network sees subgroups inside a graph. He shows it is strictly stronger than the yardsticks now in use. Those older tests rest on node counts, links, and shared subgraphs. A sharper test helps teams pick the right network for a task. He also shows a use in fair graph mining.
arxiv-2601-13651:
Marta Moscati and co-authors study how to match a face with the right voice in 2026. Face-voice association is a task in learning across senses. Systems build embeddings, compact codes for a face or a voice. Codes for the same person should sit close, and codes for others should sit far apart.

Past work used loss functions to pull and push those codes. The team adds an inductive bias aimed at maximum class separation. In plain terms, the design itself nudges classes far apart. Better face-voice matches aid media search, security checks, and tools for the blind.
arxiv-2601-14051:
Peter Devine, Mardhiyah Sanni, and Farid Adilazuarda build small language models for low-resource languages in 2026. Their pipeline, Kakugo, is novel and cost-effective by design. It takes only the language name as input to start. A large teacher model then generates synthetic prompts for that language.

The teacher also translates instruction datasets into the target language. That data trains general-purpose small language models for each tongue. They produced training data and models for fifty-four low-resource languages. Small local models could serve communities that big AI firms overlook. Small models can run on cheap phones and local rigs. That keeps tools in reach for schools and clinics with low budgets.
arxiv-2601-14151:
Jordan Barrett, Karen Gunderson, JD Nir, and Paweł Prałat study fire spread on a grid that grows in 2026. Graph burning is a discrete-time process on graphs. Vertices are activated in sequence, and burning vertices ignite their neighbours over time. The team focuses on a dynamic setting where the graph grows at each step.

Their grids expand by a function of the step count in both directions. They ask which burning densities are achievable on such growing grids. Density here means the share of vertices that can be made to burn. The model echoes firebreak and vaccination problems in growing networks.
arxiv-2601-14251:
Said Taghadouini, Adrien Cavaillès, and Baptiste Aubertin present LightOnOCR-2-1B in this 2026 paper. It is a vision-language model with one billion parameters. Its job is OCR, turning document images such as PDFs into clean text. The model works end to end, in one pass. It also handles many languages.

Older OCR tools chain many brittle steps. This model skips that chain and gives text in natural reading order. It was trained on a large, high-grade mix made by distillation, with strong coverage of scans, French documents, and science PDFs. The authors say it tops OlmOCR-Bench while being nine times smaller and much faster than past best models.
arxiv-2601-14751:
Steven Vander Eeckt and Hugo Van hamme fight forgetting in speech models in this 2026 paper. Catastrophic forgetting remains a major challenge for continual learning in automatic speech recognition. A model must adapt to new domains without losing performance on previously learned conditions. Several past methods try to penalize changes to important weights.

The team's method uses inverse-Hessian regularization. The Hessian captures how sharply the loss curves around each weight. Its inverse marks which weights can move safely. Regularization then steers learning toward those safe directions. Readers get a continual learning scheme for speech recognizers that must pick up new accents and settings without unlearning old ones.
arxiv-2601-15551:
Bismack Tokoli, Luis Jaimes, and Ayesha S. Dina present a tutoring system design in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is called ALIGNAgent. Personalized learning tools tailor content, pacing, and feedback to each student. Most current systems stay fragmented, the authors note. One tool traces knowledge, another diagnoses gaps, a third recommends resources. Few join these parts into one adaptive cycle.

ALIGNAgent is built to close that loop. Its name expands to adaptive learner intelligence for gap identification and next-step guidance. The design links diagnosis to the guidance a student gets next. A record note in the abstract lists the venue as Nuclear Physics B, an odd fit for the topic. Readers should treat that line with care. The core idea is a single agent that finds gaps and steers study.
arxiv-2601-15751:
Xinda Chen and four co-authors study how software should reason over growing tables in a 2026 arXiv paper. Tabular data is a fundamental form of data structure. Table tools trace a long arc of progress in data handling. Tables do not sit still, though. Their columns change as technology and needs shift. Data integration also merges tables with mismatched shapes. A system that reasons step by step must cope with that churn.

The title names the task: tabular incremental inference. Incremental means conclusions update as the table grows or changes. Old answers should not silently rot when a column appears. The work targets tools that analyze tables in real workflows. For data platforms, steady inference over shifting tables is a daily need, not a luxury.
arxiv-2601-15851:
A. Herle and five co-authors measure a survey contaminant in cosmic simulations in a 2026 arXiv paper. Intrinsic alignments are a major astrophysical nuisance. They affect next-generation sky surveys like Euclid and LSST. Galaxies tend to align with their surroundings, faking part of the lensing signal. Large hydrodynamic simulations help model that effect. The team uses the FLAMINGO simulation suite for the task.

They measure two-point statistics for a luminous red galaxy sample. Position-position and position-shape correlations carry the alignment signal. The record cuts off mid-claim, but the aim is clear. Survey teams must subtract alignment effects to read dark matter maps. Simulation-based estimates of the signal guide that subtraction. Better models mean cleaner cosmology from the coming surveys.
arxiv-2601-14951:
Carolin Holtermann, Nina Krebs, and Anne Lauscher test whether image generators grasp time. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with text-to-image models. Time changes how things look, from objects and places to animals.

A model that ignores time can draw the wrong scene. A landscape in spring should not match the same landscape in winter. The authors present TempViz, a way to gauge temporal knowledge in these models. The study asks how well these models use time cues, such as seasons or ages, when they build an image from a written prompt.
arxiv-2601-15151:
Jean Bruant, Pierre-Henri Horrein, Olivier Muller, and Frédéric Pétrot speed up network hardware design. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with FPGAs, chips that cloud providers use for fast packet work. These chips promise low delay and high throughput.

The snag is the slow hardware design process. It keeps FPGAs out of fast-moving infrastructure, from incident response to long-term change. The authors build a pipeline automation framework. It aims to make high-throughput network applications on FPGAs reusable, so a design can be rebuilt quickly and often rather than by hand each time.
arxiv-2601-15251:
Varshini Reddy, Craig W. Schmidt, and co-authors test whether language models can still do math when the numbers look strange. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with LLM numeracy. The models rival humans on basic arithmetic in the usual format.

But training data favors a few prevailing conventions for writing numbers. The authors probe numerical reasoning across many numeral scripts and formats. A number in Latin digits is set against the same number in Devanagari digits, among other forms. The study asks how much of the skill is real and how much is format habit.
arxiv-2601-15351:
Md Khairul Islam and Judy Fox build a foundation model for the spectra of stars and galaxies. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents OmniSpectra. Spectra are the spread of light by wavelength, and surveys now gather them in huge numbers.

Older foundation models take only fixed-length inputs in a fixed wavelength range. OmniSpectra is the first to work at native resolution. It takes spectra of any length at their original size, with no resampling or interpolation. That freedom lets one model serve data from many instruments and many large modern sky surveys.
arxiv-2601-15451:
Emily Heath, Coy Schwieder, and Shira Zerbib count colors in a coloring game on the hypercube. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with generalized Ramsey numbers. The board is the hypercube, the graph of corners of a many-dimensional cube joined by edges.

The question asks for the minimum number of colors for the edges. The coloring must give every copy of a fixed cycle at least a set number of colors. No cycle may be too plain. The authors study how that minimum grows with the cube's dimension and the cycle's length.
arxiv-2601-16251:
The RES-NOVA group tests a cold probe for dark matter hits. Their 2026 preprint reports work with a test build of the probe. The full probe will watch for rare hits from dark matter grains. Cold probes can sense the tiny heat from one such hit. Test builds must first show they run clean and quiet.

The group reports what the test probe saw in its first runs. Noise, base line and hit marks are all checked with care. Clean runs would clear the way to a full scale probe. That probe would join the hunt for dark matter mass. The work is a step in a long build chain.
arxiv-2601-16551:
Ergash Tursunov and Daniel Baye split the M1 part of a key nucleus build act. Their 2026 preprint deals with alpha plus deuteron to lithium six. That act makes lithium six with a gamma ray shed. Its M1 part is a small but key part of the rate. A trick form of the M1 step is shown to match the long wave form.

Match holds in all rate sums the team checks. The trick form lets them split the M1 part with care. Parts can then be weighed by their true weight in the rate. True rates guide star and early space maths. The work is a fine sum study of one act.
arxiv-2601-16651:
Lukas Hinterleitner, Loris Schoenegger, and Benjamin Roth ask a plain question about large language models. When a model gives an answer, which training texts shaped that answer? Their 2026 preprint tests ways to trace such links. The usual tools rely on model gradients, which are huge in size.

To cut the cost, most teams use only part of the model. That part is often picked with no clear reason. The authors check two routes in a strict way. One route picks a small set of weights. The other presses the full signal into fewer numbers. Their tests help teams pick a route with proof, not habit.
arxiv-2601-16851:
Albert Zhu, Daniel Bennett, Daniel Larson, Mohammed Al Ezzi, Efstratios Manousakis, and Efthimios Kaxiras map twisted graphene from first rules. Two sheets of carbon, turned by a hair, form new patterns. Those patterns shift how electrons move and pair. Their 2026 preprint spans a wide range of twist turns. It uses dense first-rule math with a lean base set.

The team let each twist form relax to its true shape. Turns as low as one degree come in reach. Maps of form and electron states come out. Such maps guide labs that build twist sheets by hand. They also test tales of flat-band magic in these sheets.
arxiv-2601-17151:
Qianchu Liu, Sheng Zhang, and Guanghui Qin scale AI that writes scan reports for docs. Top text bots still stumble on rich health shots. Report text is a key case of that gap. Rule-tuned training lifts scores but apes stock text. It learns the boilerplate, not the scan's truth. Their 2026 preprint turns to reward-based learn steps in place of rote fits.

Such steps mix sight and text in joint training. Rewards push reports to match scan facts. Less rote text means docs can trust drafts more. The work aims at scale, not one-off wins. Care AI needs that scale with truth kept.
arxiv-2601-17251:
Yunuo Chen and five co-authors present EMPM, a way to model soft, bendable objects. Such objects include cloth, gel, and other continuum materials. Good models must look right and act right. They must also learn from little data and work on new cases. Many past methods fail on at least one of those needs. They smooth out rich motion or need huge training sets.

EMPM aims to keep rich dynamics while staying data-light. The work sits where vision, graphics, and robotics meet. Robots need such models to handle soft goods with care. Film and game teams need them for real motion. A broad, light model could serve all three fields at once.
arxiv-2601-17451:
Nikos Georgiou, Brendan Guilfoyle, and Morgan Robson study families of oriented lines in space. They view such families as submanifolds of the tangent bundle of the sphere. One key family is lines normal to a surface. The authors show those families match ones that are isotropic for a natural structure. Isotropic here means the family sits in a null way in that structure.

That match gives a clean test for line families. Line families model light rays, robot paths, and sight lines. A firm test helps geometers sort them fast. It also links surface theory to line geometry. The focal sets of such families add more shape data. The work builds a bridge both fields can use.
arxiv-2601-17651:
Reese Lance derives higher order double point formulas with SSM-Thom polynomials. Double point loci mark where a map between complex manifolds hits one point twice. Classical formulas give the class of that locus from global data. Lance uses Segre-Schwartz-MacPherson classes to extend the story. Those classes refine older Chern class tools.

Higher order formulas capture finer overlap patterns. Maps with self-intersections arise in geometry and robotics paths. Exact classes save long local computations. Thom polynomials give universal forms for singularities. Lance's work links those universals to double points. Geometers gain formulas they can apply by substitution. The result enriches singularity theory's core toolkit.
arxiv-2601-17751:
Hong-Bae Jeon and Chan-Byoung Chae design a new kind of aerial relay for 6G wireless networks. Their 2026 preprint puts an active reflecting surface on a high platform in the sky. The surface can boost a signal as it reflects it, not just bounce it on. The goal is full three-dimensional coverage for drone base stations and for users on the ground.

Older designs of this kind covered only flat, two-dimensional areas. They also served ground users only, or worked in a passive mode with no boost. A boosted signal helps beat the fading that hits a signal twice on its path. The design aims to do all this while using energy with care.
arxiv-2601-17851:
Hua Yue, Lin Nie, Yiqing Guo, and Hongbo Hu revisit a long-standing puzzle in cosmic ray physics. Their 2026 preprint is about the knee, a bend in the cosmic ray energy spectrum. No one yet knows for sure what makes the bend. Guesses point to how the rays are sped up, how they hit other matter, or how they spread through the Galaxy.

New data give the team fresh leverage. The LHAASO observatory has measured the proton spectrum with fine care, along with total and composition spectra and the rays' direction spread. By testing models against all of these at once, the authors narrow where the knee's cause can sit. Joint use of spectrum and direction is the key move.
arxiv-2601-17951:
Yuhan Wen and co-authors look for signs that black holes starve their own galaxies. Their 2026 preprint studies quasars with moderate radio output. An active galactic nucleus pours out energy that can heat cold gas or push it out of the galaxy. Cold gas is the raw stuff of new stars, so losing it can shut star birth down. The team asks how radio activity links to the size of those gas stores.

They compare quasars across levels of radio strength. If stronger radio output pairs with thinner gas, that is a clue that feedback is at work. The title reports evidence of gas depletion in these quasars. Such clues help piece together how black holes shape the growth of galaxies over time.
arxiv-2601-18051:
Mia Kumamoto and Catherine Welch compute how neutrinos interact inside merging neutron stars when strong magnetic fields are present. Their 2026 preprint deals with neutrino opacities, which set how far neutrinos travel before they scatter. Neutrinos shape both transport and flavor change in the debris of a merger. Simulations hint that mergers can build fields as strong as 10^17 gauss. Yet computing field effects on interaction rates has been too hard to include.

The authors take on that computation directly. Better rates change how merger models predict heat, composition, and the light we see. Those predictions feed the study of how heavy elements form. The work removes a known gap in merger physics.
arxiv-2601-18251:
Kesha Ou and co-authors model how a user's interests shift over time, for better click prediction. Their 2026 preprint presents GenCI. Click-through rate prediction is pivotal in online ads and recommenders. Most models match a candidate item against the user's history. That matching can overfit to the traits that dominated the past. It then fails when interests move fast. The authors instead model interest shift in a generative way, learning intent through cohorts of similar users.

Cohort views let the model borrow strength from people with like patterns. A user whose taste is turning can be read against a cohort that already turned. Fresher intent reads should lift both ads and feeds.
arxiv-2601-19051:
Henry Chen and four co-authors harden language model systems by attacking them first, on purpose. Prompt based attacks are a chief risk when such systems go live, since user input is free form text with no fixed shape. Guards built once tend to age fast as attack tricks evolve.

Their system, HASTE, keeps forging fresh attack vectors and uses them to tune the defense while the system runs. It was shared at a security workshop tied to the NDSS symposium. A defense that trains against new attacks as they emerge fits a threat that never stands still.
arxiv-2601-19451:
Isha Pandey and three co-authors give speech recognition a team of projectors for many languages at once. New systems link frozen speech encoders to language models through light projector layers. In one language that works well, but a single projector strains to map the diverse sounds of many languages into meaning.

Their method uses dynamic multi expert projectors with stabilized routing, so each language leans on the experts that fit it. Speech tools that hold up across languages serve the many users whom English only systems leave behind. Stable routing keeps the team from collapsing onto a few overused experts.
arxiv-2601-19551:
Geunhyeok Yu and Hyoseok Hwang take on a flaw in deep learning models that refine their answers step by step. Many models stack layers, and each layer updates an internal state. Yet nothing forces those middle states to stay meaningful. That gap makes early stopping and adaptive computing shaky, since a half-finished state may be nonsense.

The authors set a structural rule: the internal dynamics should stay scale-consistent across rounds of refinement. From that rule they derive a method called FROST. It gives the state space a self-similar, fractal-like structure through a built-in bias. With that structure, partial results are more likely to be valid on their own. The work aims at models that can stop early and still be trusted.
arxiv-2601-19851:
Rayna Hata and four colleagues study how blind people share control with a navigation robot. Independent navigation is vital to daily life but hard without sight. Robots can guide users and build confidence. Yet a fully autonomous robot can leave the user feeling sidelined, even when they want to stay involved.

The authors ask how delegation in this partnership evolves over time. Early trips may need heavy robot guidance. As trust and skill grow, the balance may shift. Their study follows that changing relationship. Designing for delegation means respecting the user's wish for control. The findings guide robots that assist without taking over.
arxiv-2601-20051:
Gautham Vinod and four colleagues recover the true size of food from a single photograph. Diet-related chronic diseases like obesity and diabetes make accurate food monitoring valuable. AI dietary tools can name foods in a photo. Estimating how much food is present, the portion, is the pressing challenge, because a flat image hides scale.

Their method reconstructs real-scale three-dimensional models from monocular images. True scale turns a picture into a portion estimate. That answers the question diet tracking actually asks: how much did you eat? The reconstruction must work from one ordinary photo, not a lab scan. Better portion estimates could make nutrition apps trustworthy enough for clinical use.
arxiv-2601-20251:
Skyler Wu, Yash Nair, and Emmanuel J. Candès make the evaluation of large language models cheaper while keeping statistical guarantees. Testing many models on a large suite of benchmarks is expensive, since each test item costs a model call. The authors cast benchmarking as finite-population inference, like surveying a fixed set of items.

Under a fixed query budget, they seek tight confidence intervals for model accuracy with valid coverage. Smart sampling can then rank models without testing every item. This matters as benchmark suites grow: labs could spend less on evaluation and still know how sure each ranking is.
arxiv-2601-18551:
Paloma Thevenet and four colleagues watch the jet of a far bright galaxy core twist and swing over time. The core, named 3C 66A, shoots a thin jet of stuff at near light speed. Shots from a world web of dishes can read the jet at fine scale, close to its root. More and more such jets are seen to change their aim with time.

That change of aim can hint at a wobble in the disc that feeds the core, or at shakes in the jet it-self. The team track the jet across many dates to chart its twist and swing. A clean chart helps sort which cause fits the moves. It also feeds the tale of how cores and their discs dance as one. Such work needs long, calm watch over years.
arxiv-2601-18751:
Seyed Amir Hosseini and six colleagues tackle a flaw in a way to teach agents from side-by-side picks. In that path, a judge says which of two runs was best, and the agent learns from the pick. Real judges are a mixed lot. Some are sharp, some are sloppy, and some pick the worst run on aim. Past tools treat all picks the same, or try to drop the bad judges out.

Both paths fail when a judge is sly: their picks look like help but push the agent wrong. The team build a tool that can trust, doubt, or flip each judge's picks as it learns. A flipped pick from a sly judge turns from harm to help. Such care could make pick-based training safe in the wild, where judges can't all be vetted.
arxiv-2601-21251:
Ce Hao, Xuanran Zhai, Yaohua Liu, and Harold Soh teach robots to reuse skills across many tasks. Policies based on diffusion models do well at single manipulation tasks. Extending them to many tasks usually needs much bigger models and far more demonstrations.

Their policy mixes a small set of expert parts that share a compact skill base. A sticky routing step picks a few fitting experts for each moment of a task. Skills learned for one job can then be combined for new ones. The design aims at robots that learn broad skills without a fresh giant model for every task.
arxiv-2601-21351:
Chendong Song and seven co-authors work out the best split between two kinds of hardware in serving language models. A new serving design separates attention work from the feed-forward work after it. Attention is heavy on memory, while the other part is heavy on raw compute.

The two pools are linked at each generation step, so balance matters. Too few units on either side leaves the other side idle and slows every token. The authors derive the ratio that should work best in theory. Their result gives operators a principled way to size each pool instead of guessing.
arxiv-2601-21551:
Yang Zhou and eight co-authors improve how language models take a patient's history over several turns of talk. Good history taking is a core clinical skill, yet it is rarely tested directly. Models shine on fixed quizzes but often falter in live, turn-by-turn diagnosis.

Their method feeds the model real medical notes to guide its questions. With the notes in view, the model can refine its guesses as answers arrive. Better questioning should lead to faster, safer diagnosis support. The work treats conversation itself, not just the final answer, as the skill to train.
arxiv-2601-21651:
Savvas Panagi, Chrysovalantis Spanias, and Petros Aristidou jointly optimize heat and power in local grids filled with electric cars and heat pumps. Electrifying transport and heating gives grid operators welcome flexibility. The same devices also tie thermal and electrical behavior tightly together.

That coupling breaks the assumptions of older network management. Their framework plans both sides at once for active distribution grids. Coordinated control can shave peaks by timing charging and heating against each other. The work supports towns adding many electric vehicles and heat pumps without rebuilding the whole network.
arxiv-2601-22351:
Richard Battye and Adam Moss ask a plain question: must dark energy push the same way in all directions? Dark energy drives the late growth of the cosmos. Their 2026 preprint lets the push vary by direction and by time, in a stretched-space model.

They shape the model so a key bound from the faint early glow holds by design. That bound comes from how the glow's heat shifts as it crosses space. The work maps how much warp the data still allow. It tests a core claim of the standard cosmic story.
arxiv-2601-22551:
Meixia Lin and a large team tackle camera location across mixed devices for the CroCoDL 2025 challenge. Their 2026 preprint joins a shared retrieval encoder with two paths to a fix. One path uses classic geometry with fused features and a PnP solve; the other is a neural feed-forward model fed with geometric inputs.

Cross-device location matters when phones, drones, and robots must share one map. A hybrid that pairs classic rigor with learned speed can hold up where either alone fails. The work is a contest entry, built to a shared test.
arxiv-2601-22651:
Naoki Murata and a team assign credit for a diffusion model's output to whole groups of training data. Attribution asks which data shaped a given image. Their 2026 preprint, Guda, notes that users often need group answers — a style, a class — not one image at a time.

Group credit is a counterfactual: how would the output change if the group were gone? Their method answers by way of unlearning. Fair group credit can guide pay, consent, and data curation. The work serves artists and data holders most. It makes a vague debt concrete.
arxiv-2601-22751:
Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan and Bum Jun Kim built a physics-informed network that reads off scaling exponents as it solves. Near singularities and critical points, nature follows power laws. Their 2026 preprint notes that standard networks hide those exponents inside their weights.

Their Müntz-Szász network treats the exponents as trainable dials. It outputs both the solution and its scaling shape. Known exponents let scholars check a result against theory at a glance. The work serves physics where the exponent is the story. It makes a hidden number explicit. Clear exponents also make results easy to share.
arxiv-2601-21951:
James Matthew Young and co-authors build samplers for probability distributions that are known only up to a scaling constant. Many problems in physics and statistics have exactly that form. Diffusion-based samplers move along a path that smoothly connects a simple starting distribution to the hard target one.

The team's 2026 preprint combines that diffusion path with sequential Monte Carlo. That method carries a population of samples. It reweights them along the way. The blend aims for samples that are both accurate and efficient to draw. Better samplers feed everything from Bayesian model fitting to molecular simulation. Where the quality of conclusions is capped by the quality of the samples behind them.
arxiv-2601-22051:
Nabhanila Nandi and co-authors study thin wires where two states of matter fight. The wires join a magnet to a material that can carry power with no loss. The magnet tends to kill that loss-free state. Yet the state can live on where the pull of the magnet fades or cancels out.

Near the walls that split one magnet zone from the next, the pull drops to near zero. The loss-free state can grow there. It can also grow when many small zones mix, so that their pulls average out to near zero. The team shows how the pattern of these zones shapes where the state can live. Such wires are a test bed for new types of quantum parts.
arxiv-2601-20951:
Ashwat Jain, Wojciech Jankowski, M. Mehraeen, and Robert-Jan Slager show that some topological phases can steer sound in one direction. Their 2026 paper presents the topological acoustic diode. A diode lets a signal pass one way but not back. Here the signal is sound, and the gate is a three-dimensional topological phase. The team shows such phases realize nonlinear odd acoustoelastic effects.

Two effects stand out. One is anomalous acoustic second-harmonic generation, where sound doubles its frequency. The other is rectification, where vibration yields a steady response. Both are captured by a momentum-space tensor from quantum state geometry. The work joins topology with acoustics in a fresh way. It hints at devices that route or harvest sound using quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-21151:
Carlos Pereira and a large team of co-authors give weather models a dedicated engine for moving air. Their 2026 paper presents a neural semi-Lagrangian architecture for weather forecasting. Recent machine learning forecasters often use one monolithic network. Distinct physical mechanisms are then represented only implicitly. Advection, diffusion-like mixing, thermodynamics, and forcing all blur together. Advection suffers most from that blur. It needs long-range transport across the globe.

Treating advection implicitly demands expensive global interactions or deep convolutional stacks. A semi-Lagrangian design follows air parcels along their paths instead. That matches how the atmosphere actually moves weather. The architecture builds transport in, rather than hoping a big network learns it. The paper aims for forecasts that respect physics by construction. It joins a push for hybrid models that keep the best of both traditions.
arxiv-2512-01551:
Yunfeng Jiang and co-authors extend the rational Q-system to spin chains without U(1) symmetry. The Q-system solves Bethe ansatz equations in full. It has been a fast, complete tool. Its use was stuck to systems with that symmetry, though.

Their extension covers closed XXZ-type chains that lack it. Removing the symmetry cap widens the tool a lot. Many real integrable models lack U(1) symmetry. A complete solver for them helps in condensed matter work on magnets and cold atoms. The closed XXZ case is a proving ground, chosen since its spectrum is known well enough to expose any gap in the new frame.
arxiv-2512-01851:
Nishil Savla rebuilds the PMNS matrix with a classical pendulum system. Neutrino oscillations come from interference between mass states. The PMNS matrix governs that mixing. The effect is quantum at its core. Its math mirrors coupled classical oscillators, though.

Savla builds three pendulums linked by springs as an analog. The pendulum modes mimic three-flavor oscillation traits. A tabletop analog makes abstract mixing tangible for students. It also offers an intuitive check on how mixing angles shape oscillation patterns. Spring constants map to mixing angles, so turning a lab knob sweeps the analog through the same space neutrino fits explore.
arxiv-2512-01751:
Christian Bonatti and Theo Marty build foliations from pre-laminations on a circle. A singular foliation on the plane has a circular boundary at infinity. That boundary carries a pre-lamination structure. The forward link was known. The converse was open.

The pair solve the converse in full. They state which pre-laminations arise from a foliation. They then build the unique matching foliation. Both regular and prong-singular cases are covered. The result completes a dictionary between plane dynamics and circle data. Uniqueness matters as much as existence, since a boundary that matched two foliations would leave the dictionary ambiguous at its core.
arxiv-2512-00651:
Mohammed Latif Siddiq, Arvin Islam-Gomes, Natalie Sekerak, and Joanna Santos examine how repeatable recent software research really is. Their 2025 study covers papers that use large language models to help with software engineering tasks. Repeatable work lets other teams check results and build on them with trust.

The team mined and reviewed hundreds of papers from top venues in software, machine learning, and language work, spanning 2020 to 2025. They pulled structured details from the papers, code stores, and project notes. Their large survey gives the field a clear baseline on what authors share, and what they leave out.
arxiv-2512-00851:
Du Wenzhang wrote a 2025 paper on forecasting traffic across many cities at once. Traffic patterns differ sharply by city: road networks vary in size and shape, and data volume can differ by orders of magnitude. New cities may join with only a few weeks of logs.

Most deep traffic models are trained for one city and one backbone model at a time. Keeping a separate predictor for every city is costly. The author's city-conditioned memory gives one model a store of city-specific patterns it can draw on. That design aims to help forecasts transfer to new cities with little data.
arxiv-2512-01151:
Dong Liu proposes Fiber Bundle Networks in a 2025 machine learning paper. Most deep networks fit functions as black boxes, powerful but hard to interpret. Liu instead combines differential geometry with machine learning, recasting classification as a geometric optimization problem on fiber bundles.

In a fiber bundle, points of a base space each carry a fiber, a small space attached above them. Here, categories form the base space, and wavelet-transformed features lie in the fibers above each category. Classification then becomes a structured geometric choice rather than a blind fit. Interpretable geometry could help users see why a model sorted an item as it did.
arxiv-2601-22951:
Mayank Nautiyal and seven co-authors present OneFlowSBI, one model that answers many inference questions. Simulation-based inference learns from computer simulations when direct formulas are out of reach. Usually each question, like finding likely parameters, needs its own training run.

Their model learns the joint pattern of parameters and observations in one go. A masking trick during training lets the same model sample posteriors, estimate likelihoods, and more. One flexible model could speed up science fields that lean on heavy simulators. Query-aware masking during training is the trick that lets one trained model serve many different inference questions afterward.
arxiv-2601-23151:
Katherine Keegan and Lars Ruthotto help AI models create samples that must obey strict rules. These models work well on many tasks. But they hit a wall when each sample must meet exact equal terms, as is common in science. The sample space then forms a curved surface, and naive sampling drifts off it.

Their fix bends the samples back toward that surface in a cheap and sound way. It is built to be flexible, so it can plug into many model types. The aim is to cure known flaws of rule-bound generation. Sound samples that respect hard rules serve design, physics, and other fields where a wrong sample is useless.
arxiv-2512-00051: Amelia Fernández Seguel, an undergraduate engineering student at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, studies how magnetic forces act between tiny robots. Her project covers modeling those forces and using them to control the robots' motion. Microrobots are small machines that can be steered without direct contact, and magnetic fields are a common way to move them. The surviving record gives the topic, the author, and the program setting, but no abstract text. Her methods and results therefore cannot be described in more detail here.
arxiv-2512-00251:
Internet-of-things networks are easy targets for denial-of-service attacks, because their devices are many and often weak. Henry Onyeka and co-authors propose SD-CGAN in 2025, a framework for spotting such attacks at the network edge. Traffic there is dynamic and heavily imbalanced.

SD-CGAN is a conditional generative adversarial network enhanced with Sinkhorn divergence, tailored for anomaly detection in edge environments. It is designed to catch sophisticated attacks and zero-day exploits that known signatures miss. Reliable detection protects everyday connected devices, from cameras to sensors, that owners rarely monitor themselves. Edge deployment keeps detection close to the devices under attack, cutting response time. Generative models help because attack traffic is too varied for fixed signatures alone.
arxiv-2512-00451:
Voice calls over satellite, maritime, and tactical links are expensive because bandwidth is scarce. Siyu Wang, Haitao Li, and Donglai Zhu present STCTS in 2025, a generative semantic compression framework for speech at ultra-low bitrates. Traditional codecs struggle below one kilobit per second.

Earlier semantic approaches convert speech to text and back, sacrificing prosody and speaker identity. STCTS decomposes speech explicitly into text, prosody, and timbre, then regenerates natural voice from that compact description. Keeping the speaker's tone and identity at very low rates could change communication wherever bandwidth is precious. The target rate, around eighty bits per second, is far below ordinary telephony. Prosody carries emotion and emphasis, which text-only schemes throw away.
arxiv-2512-00551:
Equal sums of like powers form a classical Diophantine puzzle: two pairs of numbers whose powers match. Valery Asiryan studies the equation under an extra linear constraint in 2025, calling the approach the linear slicing method. The variables are nonnegative integers and the exponent is real and greater than one.

Modular and geometric constraints narrow where solutions can hide. Linear slicing cuts the search space with a condition linking the pair sums, turning a wild problem into a structured one. Such equations connect to taxicab numbers and Euler's sum of powers, small questions that have driven number theory for centuries. The linear constraint is the slicing move that gives the method its name.
arxiv-2512-03551:
Groups of users may need to prove membership all at once. Oylum Gerenli, Gunes Karabulut-Kurt, and Enver Ozdemir present a user centric group authentication scheme in this 2025 work. Group schemes verify many users simultaneously without a certification authority.

Past schemes fall into three generations based on their math foundations. The authors aim for a scheme centered on user needs for secure communication. Efficient group checks matter for chat, IoT networks, and shared workspaces. Removing a central authority can cut cost and single points of failure. User centric design aims to ease enrollment, a common pain point in group schemes.
arxiv-2512-01951:
The Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 has an infrared detector whose response bends slightly as signals grow, and astronomers correct that bend pixel by pixel. Sachindev Shenoy and co-authors revisit the correction in 2025, which rests on ground test data gathered during a thermal vacuum campaign before launch.

In the current reference file, each pixel's correction coefficients are averaged across the detector's four quadrants, smoothing away pixel-level detail. A per-pixel correction promises cleaner measurements of faint infrared sources. Work of this kind quietly underpins the accuracy of every infrared image the camera delivers, long after its ground tests ended.
arxiv-2512-02051:
If two whole-plane functions share enough values, must they be one and the same? Jeet Sarkar and Debabrata Pramanik chase this question in 2025. They compare a function with a shifted form built from its own rate of change.

Such sameness theorems are core tools in the study of how functions spread their values. They tell when data pin a function down in full. The pair prove three results. Each one sharpens and broadens a 2011 theorem by Qi. Stronger rules help analysts see when shifted forms, common in difference equations, cannot pose as each other.
arxiv-2512-02251:
Farmers adapting to climate change need answers that are both scientifically accurate and readable, and those answers are scattered across papers and government data feeds. Liangji Kong, Aditya Joshi, and Sarvnaz Karimi present CAIRNS in 2025, a question-answering system for climate adaptation that tries to hold both virtues at once.

Adaptation strategies for sustaining food production live in unstructured literature and in structured climate data from official sources. A system that can draw on both must phrase findings plainly without flattening their accuracy. Balancing readability against precision is the central design problem, and it decides whether farmers and advisors can actually use the answers.
arxiv-2512-02151:
Integrating an increasing function once gives its accumulated area; integrating the result again and again builds a tower of smoother curves. Maxim Burke and co-authors characterize in 2025 exactly which triples of values those repeated integrals can take at the endpoint, for increasing functions on the unit interval.

The question grew out of a problem about approximating smooth functions by entire functions in a comonotone way, keeping the same increasing pattern. Knowing the reachable set of first, second, and third integral values draws the boundary of what such functions can do. Results of this kind are the fine print of approximation theory, where they decide which approximation schemes can exist.
arxiv-2512-02351:
Unified multimodal models pack understanding and generation into one system, but most tasks use only a slice of that bulk. Shwai He and three co-authors study in 2025 how sparsity, running only the needed parts, can cure the inefficiency that unification creates.

A question about a picture may not need the model's generation machinery, and a caption may not need its deepest reasoning. Identifying and harnessing that sparsity means routing each task or sample to the capacity it actually requires. The work points toward unified models that keep their versatility without charging every user for all of it.
arxiv-2512-02551:
Songqiao Su and five co-authors attack matrix multiplication, the core math inside large language models. Fast multiplication kernels are hard to tune by hand. Each matrix shape rewards a different strategy, and tricks that help on one graphics chip often fail on another.

Their system, CUDA-L2, uses reinforcement learning to search for fast kernels on its own. The learning agent tests variants and keeps what runs fastest, aiming past the standard cuBLAS library. Automatic tuning at scale could speed up AI training and serving, where multiplication dominates both time and energy cost. Speed gains here flow straight to the cost of each task a firm runs on its chips.
arxiv-2512-02751:
Rakib Ahsan and three co-authors spot methane plumes from space with an attention based neural network. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and fast detection of leaks allows timely repair. Satellite images from Sentinel-2 already watch the whole planet on a regular cycle.

AttMetNet adds attention layers that teach the network where a faint plume is likely to hide. The framework targets plumes in Sentinel-2 imagery specifically. Automated detection at scale could help governments and firms find super emitters, a small set of sources behind much of the methane problem. Most leaks come from a few bad sites, so a fast sky scan is the quick way to find the worst ones first.
arxiv-2512-03051:
Ocean models stumble at coastlines, where their grids simply end. Treating fields near domain boundaries is a long standing problem in signal processing. New convolution based coarse graining methods and machine learned parameterizations have revived it, since both create artifacts at ocean boundaries.

The proposed method extends fields beyond the boundary by solving a Laplace boundary value problem. That harmonic extension is general and principled, not an ad hoc patch. Cleaner boundaries improve multiscale analysis and learned ocean models, where coastal errors now leak into open water forecasts. Coasts are where most of us live and work. Coast wise marks in a sea model are worth more than their share of grid points would first suggest to a glance.
plos-pone-0010051:
Nishit Doshi and Samir Mitragotri asked a simple question in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Macrophages are immune cells that swallow invading germs and debris. Most work on how they spot targets focused on surface receptors. The pair wondered whether sheer size and shape also guide recognition.

Using plastic particles of different shapes and sizes, they tested what macrophages take up. Their title gives the answer: these cells do recognize size and shape. That finding matters for designing drug-carrying particles that either avoid macrophages or seek them out on purpose.
plos-pone-0010151:
The authors were Christina Ting, Tarek Rajji, Zahinoor Ismail, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study compared thinking profiles in older clinic patients. Patients came to a hospital memory clinic at a center for addiction and mental health. The team compared older people with schizophrenia against those with Alzheimer's disease or depression in late life.

Using demographic, clinical, and test data, they mapped how each group's cognition differed. Telling these profiles apart helps doctors avoid mixing up very different conditions. Clearer profiles can guide care and spare families the wrong diagnosis at a difficult stage of life.
plos-pone-0010251:
The authors were Tale Sliedrecht, Chao Zhang, Kevan Shokat, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used a chemical trick to switch off a mitosis protein. Correct cell division needs chromosomes attached firmly to spindle fibers. A checkpoint delays division until every chromosome is stably attached, guarding against cells with wrong chromosome counts.

The team built stable human cell lines where the kinase Mps1 could be blocked chemically. Turning Mps1 off at chosen moments revealed new aspects of its job in mitosis. A timed off-switch gives finer answers than removing a protein for good.
plos-pone-0010351:
Bethany Cool, Guy Chan, Lin Lee and others described a mouse brain gene variant in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, Gprc5b, makes a receptor whose exact job is still unknown. It switches on in response to retinoic acid, a vitamin A relative. Many receptor genes come in several spliced forms, each slightly different. This study began with a puzzle about a neighboring gene.

Chasing that puzzle led the team to a new spliced form of Gprc5b. The form shows up mainly in the brain of one common lab mouse strain. It also appears as neurons mature. A strain-specific form can confuse studies that assume all lab mice match. More broadly, it shows how hidden gene versions shape brain biology.
plos-pone-0009851:
Estrogen protects brain cells, but not all of that protection flows through the cell nucleus. Li-cai Yang and colleagues traced the outside-the-nucleus route in the rat hippocampus. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The hippocampus handles memory and is sensitive to hormones.

Extranuclear estrogen receptors sit outside the nucleus, on or near the cell surface. The team showed these receptors mediate estrogen's neuroprotective effects in this memory region. Fast, surface-level signals can guard neurons without changing gene activity first. The finding refines how scientists picture hormone protection in the brain.
plos-pone-0009951:
Muscle fibers come in fast and slow types, and a single gene helps choose between them. Mary Lou Beermann and colleagues studied that gene switch in bird muscle grown in the lab. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The gene is Prdm1, also called Blimp-1. The team tracked its link to the fast and slow forms of myosin heavy chain. Isoforms are variant forms of the same protein. Watching the switch during avian myogenesis, muscle building in birds, clarifies how fiber types form. Muscle type decides speed and stamina.
